---
title: "Two Rankings from One Posterior: A Bayesian Power Rating and a Wins-Above-Bubble Resume for College Basketball"
abstract: "A college basketball ranking is asked two questions: which team is better, and which has earned a place in the tournament. The first is predictive and should use margin of victory; the second is retrodictive and should reward only results. We answer both from one Bayesian model. Team strength, in points per 100 possessions against an average Division I team on a neutral floor, is observed through the regulation margin and a luck-adjusted efficiency margin built from a shot-quality model and shooters' free-throw rates, modelled jointly so that one performance is not counted twice and weighted by the number of possessions. Strength is pooled within conferences, carried over between seasons through a preseason regression on last season's rating, a public preseason rating and roster turnover, and allowed to drift week to week as a random walk. The power rating is the posterior of strength. The resume, Wins Above Bubble, counts the wins a team has beyond those the last at-large team in the field would expect against the same schedule, where in each posterior draw the automatic bids leave the ranking before the bubble is found. We evaluate the system on every week of every season since 2014--15 with convergence gates, posterior predictive and prior-sensitivity checks, simulation-based calibration, ablations, and a rolling out-of-sample backtest against results, closing betting lines and totals, a public rating system and a least-squares baseline, and compare the resume with the selection committee's choices."
date: last-modified

```{r, setup}
library(knitr)

# Rendered from the project root by tar_quarto(); fall back to the parent otherwise.
root <- if (file.exists("_targets.R")) "." else ".."
store <- file.path(root, "_targets")

# Colour encodes the product and nothing else: Power in orange, Resume in blue,
# the betting market and every reference in grey. Emphasis is weight, not hue.
col_power <- "#D1622A"
col_resume <- "#3A6EA5"
col_ink <- "#202020"
col_ref <- "gray55"
col_faint <- "gray85"

theme_paper <- function(base_size = 10) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray92", linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = "gray30"),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "gray30"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, colour = col_ink),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
}
theme_set(theme_paper())

fmt <- function(v, d = 0) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
# Inside $...$ a bare comma is punctuation; {,} typesets a digit separator.
fmtm <- function(v, d = 0) gsub(",", "{,}", fmt(v, d), fixed = TRUE)
pct <- function(v, d = 0) paste0(fmt(100 * v, d), "\\%")
esc <- function(x) gsub("&", "\\&", x, fixed = TRUE)
ktab <- function(df, ...) {
  kable(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, ...)
}
# Seasons are named by the year of their tournament; in text, 2026 is "2025--26"
sl <- function(s) sprintf("%d--%02d", as.integer(s) - 1L, as.integer(s) %% 100L)
ord <- function(n) { n <- round(n); paste0(n, ifelse(n %% 100 %in% 11:13, "th", c("th", "st", "nd", "rd", rep("th", 6))[n %% 10 + 1])) }
ll <- function(p, y) -(y * log(pmax(p, 1e-6)) + (1 - y) * log(pmax(1 - p, 1e-6)))
crps_normal <- function(y, mu, s) { z <- (y - mu) / s; s * (z * (2 * pnorm(z) - 1) + 2 * dnorm(z) - 1 / sqrt(pi)) }
```

```{r, data}
# Literal target names, so that tar_quarto() registers each as a dependency
cfg <- targets::tar_read(cfg, store = store)
TEMPO <- local({ e <- new.env(); sys.source(file.path(root, "R/03_model.R"), e); e$TEMPO })
snapshots <- targets::tar_read(snapshots, store = store)
bt <- targets::tar_read(backtest, store = store)
cov <- targets::tar_read(coverage, store = store)
venues <- targets::tar_read(venues, store = store)
shot_cal <- targets::tar_read(shot_calibration, store = store)
last_full <- targets::tar_read(last_full, store = store)

params <- snapshots$params |>
  left_join(snapshots$gates |> select(season, snap_date, max_rhat, min_ess, divergences, min_ebfmi, worst, pass),
            by = c("season", "snap_date"))
seasons <- sort(unique(params$season))
prior_season <- min(seasons)            # fitted once, at its end, for the carry-over
first_season <- prior_season + 1L
current <- max(seasons)
complete <- first_season:last_full
fit_snaps <- params |> filter(season >= first_season)
n_snap <- nrow(fit_snaps)
n_pass <- sum(fit_snaps$pass)
final <- params |> filter(kind == "final")
final_full <- final |> filter(season %in% complete)

rat <- snapshots$ratings
res <- snapshots$resume
ap <- snapshots$polls |> filter(poll == "AP") |> select(season, snap_date, team_id, ap_rank = rank)
# Integer ranks for publication: by posterior mean rating and by posterior mean WAB
board <- rat |>
  left_join(res |> select(-team, -conf, -kind), by = c("season", "snap_date", "team_id")) |>
  left_join(ap, by = c("season", "snap_date", "team_id")) |>
  group_by(season, snap_date) |>
  mutate(power_rank = rank(-rating, ties.method = "first"),
         resume_rank = ifelse(is.na(wab), NA_integer_, rank(-wab, ties.method = "first")),
         colley_rank = ifelse(is.na(colley), NA_integer_, rank(-colley, ties.method = "first")),
         sor_rank = ifelse(is.na(sor), NA_integer_, rank(sor, ties.method = "first"))) |>
  ungroup()
fin_last <- board |> filter(season == last_full, kind == "final")
sel_last <- board |> filter(season == last_full, kind == "selection")
sel_date <- unique(sel_last$snap_date)

# Backtest, complete seasons only (the live season is in the store too)
btg <- bt$games |> filter(season %in% complete)
score_bt <- function(d) {
  d |> summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(actual - pred_margin)), rmse = sqrt(mean((actual - pred_margin)^2)),
                 crps = mean(crps_normal(actual, pred_margin, pred_sd)), brier = mean((p_home - home_win)^2),
                 logloss = mean(ll(p_home, home_win)), accuracy = mean((p_home > 0.5) == (home_win == 1)),
                 sharp = mean(abs(p_home - 0.5)), .groups = "drop")
}
bt_all <- score_bt(btg)
lined <- btg |> filter(!is.na(line))
bt_line <- lined |> summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(actual - pred_margin)), mae_line = mean(abs(actual - line)),
                              brier = mean((p_home - home_win)^2), brier_line = mean((p_line - home_win)^2),
                              logloss = mean(ll(p_home, home_win)), logloss_line = mean(ll(p_line, home_win)))
tv_games <- btg |> filter(!is.na(pred_torvik), !is.na(line))
bt_tv <- tv_games |> summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(actual - pred_margin)), mae_tv = mean(abs(actual - pred_torvik)),
                               mae_line = mean(abs(actual - line)), logloss = mean(ll(p_home, home_win)),
                               logloss_tv = mean(ll(p_torvik, home_win)))
tot <- btg |> filter(!is.na(total_line), !is.na(pred_total))
bt_tot <- tot |> summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(actual_total - pred_total)), mae_line = mean(abs(actual_total - total_line)))

# The Gaussian information calculation of @sec-info at each complete season's final posterior
# mean, per game at the reference length of 70 possessions
info <- final_full |>
  transmute(season, lambda, kappa, sigma_eff, sigma_m,
            S11 = sigma_eff^2, S12 = kappa * sigma_eff^2, S22 = sigma_m^2 + kappa^2 * sigma_eff^2,
            i_y = 1 / S22,
            i_joint = lambda^2 / sigma_eff^2 + (1 - kappa * lambda)^2 / sigma_m^2,
            gain = i_joint / i_y - 1,
            lambda_star = S12 / S22,
            r2 = kappa^2 * sigma_eff^2 / S22)

field_size_now <- if (last_full >= cfg$field76_from) 76L else 68L
n_games_d1 <- sum(cov$d1_played[cov$season %in% complete])
n_games_nd <- sum(cov$nond1_played[cov$season %in% complete])
poss_ref <- cfg$poss_ref
```

```{r, analyses}
# Final-snapshot refits: the published model's checks

ppc_all <- map_dfr(ff_pub, \(x) mutate(x$ppc, season = x$season))
sens_all <- map_dfr(ff_pub, \(x) mutate(x$sensitivity, season = x$season)) |> filter(!is.na(variable))
flag_counts <- sens_all |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(prior = median(prior), likelihood = median(likelihood),
            conflict = sum(grepl("conflict", diagnosis)), weak = sum(grepl("weak", diagnosis)),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop")
n_flagged_any <- sum(flag_counts$conflict + flag_counts$weak > 0)
loo_tab <- map_dfr(ff_pub, \(x) tibble(season = x$season, games = x$n_games, elpd = x$loo["elpd_loo", "Estimate"],
                                       se = x$loo["elpd_loo", "SE"], p_loo = x$loo["p_loo", "Estimate"],
                                       bad_k = sum(x$pareto_k > 0.7), pass = x$pass))
fam_ppc <- map_dfr(Filter(\(x) x$model != "margin_only", ff), \(x) mutate(x$ppc, season = x$season, model = x$model))
cmp_eff <- fcmp$per_season |> filter(model == "published", reference == "margin_only")

# Paired comparison of two sets of game scores, standard errors clustered by snapshot
paired <- function(a, b, metric) {
  j <- inner_join(a |> select(season, game_id, snap_date, x = all_of(metric)),
                  b |> select(season, game_id, y = all_of(metric)), by = c("season", "game_id"))
  d <- j$x - j$y
  u <- tapply(d - mean(d), paste(j$season, j$snap_date), sum)
  c(diff = mean(d), se = sqrt(sum(u^2)) / length(d), n = length(d))
}

# Ablations: every variant predicts the same games
abl <- abl |> mutate(err_abs = abs(err))
abl_seasons <- sort(unique(abl$season))
abl_pub <- abl |> filter(variant == "Published model")
abl_sum <- abl |> group_by(variant) |>
  summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(err_abs), brier = mean(brier), logloss = mean(logloss), .groups = "drop")
abl_diff <- map_dfr(setdiff(unique(abl$variant), "Published model"), function(v) {
  a <- abl |> filter(variant == v)
  map_dfr(c("err_abs", "brier", "logloss"), function(m) {
    x <- paired(a, abl_pub, m)
    tibble(variant = v, metric = m, diff = x[["diff"]], se = x[["se"]])
  })
})
abl_d <- function(v, m) abl_diff |> filter(variant == v, metric == m)
ablation_order <- c("Published model", "Margin only", "Shot-quality efficiency", "No preseason information",
                    "No two-season carry-over", "No conference level", "Static ratings", "No non-D1 games",
                    "Student-t margin", "Contaminated-normal margin")

# Baselines on the same games as the published predictions
pub_sc <- btg |> transmute(season, game_id, snap_date, err_abs = abs(actual - pred_margin),
                           brier = (p_home - home_win)^2, logloss = ll(p_home, home_win))
mass <- base_sc |> transmute(season, game_id, snap_date, err_abs = abs(err), brier, logloss)
mass_cmp <- inner_join(mass, pub_sc, by = c("season", "game_id"), suffix = c("_b", "_m"))
tv_sc <- btg |> filter(!is.na(pred_torvik)) |>
  transmute(season, game_id, snap_date, err_abs = abs(actual - pred_torvik), brier = (p_torvik - home_win)^2,
            logloss = ll(p_torvik, home_win))
ext_cor <- ext |> mutate(net = adj_o - adj_d) |>
  inner_join(rat |> filter(kind == "final") |> select(season, team_id, rating), by = c("season", "team_id")) |>
  group_by(season) |> summarise(rho = cor(net, rating, method = "spearman"), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Leave-one-season-out priors in the first snapshots, against the published predictions of the same games
loso_cmp <- inner_join(loso |> transmute(season, game_id, snap_date, e_l = abs(err), b_l = brier, l_l = logloss),
                       pub_sc |> select(season, game_id, e_m = err_abs, b_m = brier, l_m = logloss), by = c("season", "game_id"))

# Parameter names, as LaTeX for tables and plotmath for figures
sym_lab <- c(hca = "\\eta", b_prev = "\\beta", b_prev2 = "\\beta_2", lambda = "\\lambda", kappa = "\\kappa",
             sigma_eff = "\\sigma_e", sigma_m = "\\sigma_m", sigma_conf = "\\omega", sigma_team = "\\tau",
             tau = "\\phi", nu = "\\nu", `r_nd_raw[1]` = "m_{\\mathrm{nd}}", `sigma_nd_raw[1]` = "\\sigma_{\\mathrm{nd}}",
             sigma_game = "\\bar\\sigma", p_out = "p_o", k_out = "k_o")
var_tex <- setNames(paste0("$", sym_lab, "$"), names(sym_lab))
pm_lab <- c(hca = "eta", b_prev = "beta", b_prev2 = "beta[2]", lambda = "lambda", kappa = "kappa",
            sigma_eff = "sigma[e]", sigma_m = "sigma[m]", sigma_conf = "omega", sigma_team = "tau", tau = "phi")
sym_list <- function(v) {
  s <- paste0("$", sym_lab[v], "$")
  if (length(s) <= 1) return(s)
  paste(paste(s[-length(s)], collapse = ", "), "and", s[length(s)])
}

# Selection Monday refits: the benchmark, SOR and Monte Carlo errors
sel_bench <- map_dfr(selr, "bench")
sel_field <- map_dfr(selr, \(x) mutate(x$field, season = x$season))
bench_cmp <- sel_bench |>
  group_by(season) |>
  group_modify(function(d, k) {
    b0 <- d |> filter(benchmark == "Last team in (published)")
    d |> filter(benchmark != "Last team in (published)") |>
      group_by(benchmark) |>
      group_modify(function(e, kk) {
        j <- inner_join(e, b0, by = "team_id", suffix = c("", "_0"))
        tibble(rho = cor(j$wab, j$wab_0, method = "spearman"),
               pick_changes = sum(j$picked & !j$picked_0),
               overlap = sum(j$picked & j$at_large), overlap_0 = sum(j$picked_0 & j$at_large_0),
               bench_rank = e$bench_rank[1])
      })
  }) |> ungroup()
bench_pub <- sel_bench |> filter(benchmark == "Last team in (published)") |>
  group_by(season) |> summarise(overlap = sum(picked & at_large), at_large = sum(at_large), bench_rank = bench_rank[1], .groups = "drop")
sor_cmp <- map_dfr(selr, "sor") |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(max_diff = max(abs(sor_mean_pi - sor_per_draw)), rho = cor(sor_mean_pi, sor_per_draw, method = "spearman"), .groups = "drop")
mcse_all <- map_dfr(selr, "mcse")

# Schedule graph
sg_first <- sg |> filter(teams > 0) |> group_by(season) |>
  summarise(first_conn = min(snap_date[components == 1]), first_snap = min(snap_date), .groups = "drop")
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Every winter some 360 Division I men's basketball teams play about thirty games each, and in March a committee chooses the 68 teams of the national tournament: one automatic bid for each conference champion, the rest "at large". The schedule graph is denser than in football --- a team plays fewer than a tenth of the other teams, many of them twice within its conference, and November and December link the conferences through hundreds of non-conference games --- but the information in a single game is small. A basketball game is a sequence of some seventy possessions each way, and its margin is the difference of two noisy sums. Any ranking has to propagate strength through the graph and decide how much of each result is noise. The history of the problem is largely the history of ways to do so: least squares on scoreboard margin [@harvilleUseLinearmodelMethodology1977; @masseyStatisticalModelsApplied1997], paired-comparison models for wins and losses [@bradleyRankAnalysisIncomplete1952], linear-algebraic record-only schemes such as the Colley matrix [@colleyColleysBiasFree2002; @langvilleWhosNumberOne2012], and the tempo-free efficiency ratings that now dominate public analysis of the college game [@pomeroyRatingsExplanation2016; @torvikTRank2026], built on the possession accounting of @oliverBasketballPaperRules2004 and @kubatkoStartingPointAnalyzing2007.

These methods disagree partly because they answer different questions. A *predictive* rating asks which team would win a game played tonight, and by how much. Margin is informative about that, so a predictive rating should use it, together with any other signal of how well a team played. A *retrodictive* ranking asks what a team has earned by its results, and is the question a selection committee is asked. Here margin is usually excluded on purpose, so that a team is neither rewarded for running up a score nor penalised for resting its starters, and a win over a strong opponent is worth more than a win over a weak one. The committee's own team sheets combine both kinds of number --- a predictive rating, quadrant records, and since 2024--25 "wins above bubble" [@ncaaNETTeamSheets2024] --- and leave the weighing to its members.

This paper keeps the two questions apart but derives both answers from one posterior distribution. The contributions are four.

1. A **power model** (@sec-power) for team strength in points per 100 possessions against an average Division I team on a neutral floor, observed through the regulation scoreboard margin and through a *luck-adjusted* efficiency margin: actual two-point baskets, expected three-point baskets from a shot-quality model, and expected free throws from each shooter's prior free-throw rate. The margin is modelled *conditionally* on the efficiency residual, so the two signals share one latent strength without being treated as independent evidence, and their relative weight is estimated rather than set. Each game is weighted by its number of possessions. Strength is pooled within conferences, carried over from the previous season through a preseason regression on last season's rating, a public preseason rating and the roster's turnover, and moves through the season as a random walk whose step size is estimated. A ridge model for possessions and points per possession turns the per-100 ratings into spreads and totals in points, and splits each rating into offence and defence (@sec-tempo).
2. A result on how much the efficiency signal adds (@sec-info). Under a Gaussian version of the model the gain in per-game Fisher information about strength has a closed form, and at the fitted parameters it is `r pct(min(info$gain), 0)`--`r pct(max(info$gain), 0)` --- about `r fmt(median(info$gain) * 30, 0)` extra games' worth over a season. An ablation backtest measures the same thing out of sample (@sec-ablation).
3. A **resume** measure, Wins Above Bubble (@sec-resume): for each posterior draw, the number of wins a team has beyond those the draw's last at-large team would be expected to earn against the same opponents at the same venues. The bubble is found as the committee would find it: in each draw the conference champions --- the automatic bids, known or simulated --- and the teams not yet eligible for the tournament leave the power ranking, and the bubble team is the last of the at-large places among the rest. The measure is additive over games, never rewards a loss, is centred at zero for a team exactly as strong as the bubble, and inherits uncertainty in the opponents, the bubble and the ranks directly from the posterior.
4. A **validation** of the whole system (@sec-computation, @sec-checks, @sec-backtest) on every week of every season from `r sl(first_season)` to `r sl(last_full)`: `r fmt(n_snap)` posteriors fitted by the No-U-Turn sampler, of which `r fmt(n_pass)` pass the convergence gates; posterior predictive checks, prior-sensitivity diagnostics, simulation-based calibration, ablations and baselines; and a rolling backtest of `r fmt(bt_all$games)` games, each predicted from the posterior fitted before it, scored against the result, the closing betting line and the ratings of a public system at the same date. The resume is compared with the committee's at-large selections in every season with a tournament (@sec-validate-resume).

@fig-overview shows how these pieces fit together. @sec-data describes the data, @sec-power and @sec-info the power model, and @sec-resume the resume and the reference rankings. @sec-computation describes fitting and the pipeline, @sec-checks model checking, @sec-backtest the out-of-sample evaluation, @sec-results the `r sl(last_full)` season as a worked example, and @sec-discussion the limitations.

Structure of the paper. One posterior per snapshot date feeds both products; the dashed arrow is the only link between them: the Resume values results using opponent and bubble strengths drawn from the Power posterior, but never uses margin. Each box names the section where it is developed.
:::

**Related work.** The margin model descends from @harvilleUseLinearmodelMethodology1977 and @harvillePredictionsNationalFootball1980, who fit mixed linear models to scoreboard margin with random team effects, and from @sternProbabilityWinningFootball1991, who showed that margins are close to normal around the betting line, so that a spread determines a win probability. For college basketball specifically, @harvilleHomeCourtAdvantageHow1994 estimated the home-court advantage and its variation between teams, @kvamLogisticRegressionMarkov2006 and @lopezBuildingNCAAMens2015 built tournament prediction models from regular-season results, and @colemanIdentifyingNCAATournament2001 modelled the committee's at-large choices from the team-sheet criteria. @glickmanStatespaceModelNational1998 made team strengths evolve over time in a Bayesian state-space model; the weekly random walk here is a version of theirs, and dynamic paired-comparison models [@glickmanParameterEstimationLarge1999; @knorrheldDynamicRatingSports2000] let strengths drift between games in the same way. The tempo-free ratings of @pomeroyRatingsExplanation2016 and @torvikTRank2026 measure offence and defence per possession and adjust for opponents and venue by iterative least squares; Torvik's ratings, archived by date, serve here both as an input to the preseason rating and as a benchmark in the backtest, and Torvik also publishes a wins-above-bubble measure, against which ours is compared (@sec-validate-resume). Wins Above Bubble differs from the strength of record of the team sheets in its reference team and in how uncertainty enters; @lopezHowOftenDoes2018 quantify how much of a season's outcome is noise, which is the reason a resume should report its uncertainty. The workflow follows @gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020.

## Notation {#sec-notation}

@tbl-notation collects the notation. Games are indexed by $g$, teams by $i$ and $j$, conferences by $c$, and the model's time periods (weeks of seven days from the first game of the season) by $w$. Game $g$ is played in period $w(g)$. Posterior draws are indexed by $s = 1, \ldots, S$, and a superscript $(s)$ marks a quantity evaluated at draw $s$. A team's rating without a period index, $r_i$, is its rating at the date of the snapshot being published. Ratings and margins in the model are per 100 possessions; spreads and totals are in points.

```{r}

) |>
```

# Data {#sec-data}

Games, box scores and play-by-play come from ESPN through the bulk files of the SportsDataverse project [@sportsdataverse2026]: every game of every Division I team from `r sl(prior_season)` to `r sl(current)`, with team box scores and, for most games, play-by-play with shot locations. The CollegeBasketballData.com API [@cbbd2026] supplies the scores by half, conferences, closing betting lines (spread and over/under), NCAA tournament seeds, polls and recruiting ranks, and maps its games to ESPN's. Bart Torvik's site [@torvikTRank2026] supplies preseason ratings, the site's ratings as they stood on any past date (its "time machine"), and player tables with minutes and box plus-minus. Division I membership by season comes from ESPN; teams moving up from Division II, which are ineligible for the tournament for several seasons, and teams under a postseason ban are kept in hand-maintained tables. Teams are keyed by ESPN's identifiers throughout. The following derived quantities enter the model.

**Possessions.** The number of possessions in a game is estimated from the box score as the average over the two teams of field-goal attempts minus offensive rebounds plus turnovers plus 0.475 times free-throw attempts [@oliverBasketballPaperRules2004; @pomeroyRatingsExplanation2016]. For an overtime game the regulation possessions $n_g$ are the total scaled by the share of playing time in regulation, $40/(40 + 5k)$ for $k$ overtimes.

**Regulation margin.** $y_g = 100\,(\text{home} - \text{away})/n_g$, the home team's margin after 40 minutes per 100 regulation possessions. A game decided in overtime (`r pct(sum(cov$ot[cov$season %in% complete]) / n_games_d1, 1)` of Division I games) contributes a margin of zero: the teams were level after regulation, and the overtime is a short and different game. The win still counts as a win in the resume.

**Efficiency margin.** For each side, the *luck-adjusted* points are the points actually scored on two-point field goals, plus the *expected* points of its three-point attempts, plus the *expected* points of its free throws, all in live play: regulation time outside garbage time. A three-point attempt is worth three times its probability of being made under a shot model (below), and a free throw its shooter's free-throw rate in all earlier games, this season and last, shrunk towards the league rate as if the shooter had `r 40` more attempts at it. The efficiency margin is
$$
e_g = 100\,\frac{\text{lux}_{h(g)} - \text{lux}_{a(g)}}{n^{\mathrm{live}}_g},
$$
per 100 live possessions, with $n^{\mathrm{live}}_g$ the regulation possessions scaled by the share of regulation before garbage time began. The idea is to keep what a team controls --- the shots it takes and allows, its two-point finishing --- and to replace by their expectations the two quantities that are most variable from game to game and least repeatable: whether the threes go in, and how the free throws fall. A defence decides which threes it allows far more than whether they go in. A pure shot-quality margin, which values *every* field goal at its expected value, was built as well; it is compared in the ablations (@sec-ablation). The efficiency margin is used when both teams' shots are in the play-by-play and the game has at least 20 live possessions, and is missing otherwise.

**Shot model.** The make probability of a field-goal attempt comes from two logistic regressions, one for two-point and one for three-point attempts, on a natural spline in shot distance (four and three degrees of freedom), the kind of shot (jumper, layup, dunk, tip, hook; for twos), whether it is a putback within four seconds of an offensive rebound and whether it comes within eight seconds of a change of possession. Distance comes from the shot coordinates or the play text, capped at 30 feet and imputed by the median of its kind when missing. The model for a season is trained on the two previous seasons' shots only, so the efficiency margin of a game never uses its own result. @tbl-shots shows its calibration out of sample. Only the three-point predictions enter the published efficiency margin; the two-point ones are used only by the shot-quality variant of @sec-ablation. ESPN labels hook shots as such only from `r sl(2026)`, so that season's model learned them from a few hundred earlier labels, nearly all of made shots; the hook row's gap is that season's.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shots
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample calibration of the shot model: predicted against actual make rate by kind of shot, all field-goal attempts of the complete seasons, each season predicted by the model trained on the two before it. The largest season gap is over seasons with at least 1,000 attempts of the kind."
shot_cal |>
  filter(season %in% complete) |>
  group_by(family) |>
  summarise(pred = weighted.mean(pred, shots), actual = weighted.mean(actual, shots),
            worst = max(abs(diff[shots >= 1000])), shots = sum(shots), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(shots)) |>
  transmute(Kind = family, Attempts = fmt(shots), Predicted = pct(pred, 1), Actual = pct(actual, 1),
            `Largest season gap` = paste0(fmt(100 * worst, 1), " pts")) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrr")
```

**Garbage time.** Play in the second half counts as garbage time from the moment one team leads by 20 or more with ten minutes or fewer left, or by 15 or more with five minutes or fewer. The efficiency margin excludes it; the scoreboard margin cannot.

**Venue.** The site $\delta_g$ is $+1$ when the game is on the home team's floor, $-1$ when it is on the away team's, and 0 at a neutral site. ESPN's neutral-site flag is the starting point, with one correction: a "neutral" game played at a venue where one of the teams played at least two non-neutral home games that season or the previous one is that team's home game (`r fmt(sum(cov$site_recoded[cov$season %in% complete], na.rm = TRUE))` games over the complete seasons, mostly early-season events and conference-tournament games played on one team's own floor).

**Opponents outside Division I.** Games against Division II, III and NAIA teams (`r fmt(n_games_nd)` over the complete seasons) enter through their regulation margin only, against one pooled level for all such opponents with an extra spread for the mixture of divisions (@sec-hierarchy). They have no efficiency margin, since the play-by-play of these games is rarely complete.

**Preseason information.** Three quantities from before the season enter each team's preseason level (@sec-hierarchy): our own final rating of the team last season; Torvik's preseason rating, from the site's archive the day before opening night; and roster turnover from its player tables --- the value of returning players (box plus-minus times minutes share last season), of incoming transfers at their previous teams, of departing players, the minutes shares of returners and transfers, and the number of highly rated freshmen. They are combined by a regression of each past season's final rating on these quantities, fitted on earlier seasons only (@sec-hierarchy), and our final rating two seasons back enters the model separately.

**Snapshots.** A posterior is fitted on opening night (prior only), on every Monday from the first after the opening slate, and on the day after the championship game. The Monday before the tournament is Selection Monday. Each snapshot uses exactly the games played before its date and predicts the Division I games until the next snapshot.

**Unusual seasons.** The `r sl(2020)` season stopped during the conference tournaments, and no national tournament was held. In `r sl(2021)` most arenas were empty or nearly so, many games were cancelled or postponed, and the season had about a quarter fewer games than usual; its home-court advantage has its own prior (@sec-priors).

**Missing efficiency.** The efficiency margin is missing for `r pct(1 - sum(cov$eff_share[cov$season %in% complete] * cov$d1_played[cov$season %in% complete]) / n_games_d1)` of Division I games over the complete seasons, from `r pct(1 - max(cov$eff_share[cov$season %in% complete]), 1)` in the best-covered season to `r pct(1 - min(cov$eff_share[cov$season %in% complete]), 0)` in the worst, mostly the earliest. Whether ESPN recorded a game's shots depends on the broadcaster and the season, which are unrelated to how the game went, so the data are missing at random in the sense of @rubinInferenceMissingData1976 and the likelihood of the observed data (@eq-lik-marg for these games) is the right one to use without modelling why the efficiency margin is missing.

@tbl-data summarises the data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Data by season (named by the year of its tournament). \\emph{Teams}: Division I teams; \\emph{ineligible}: of these, those not eligible for the tournament (moving up to Division I, or banned). \\emph{Games}: completed Division I games and games against non-Division I opponents. \\emph{Eff.}, \\emph{Line}: shares of Division I games with an efficiency margin and with a closing line. \\emph{Snap.}: posteriors fitted."
cov |>
  left_join(params |> count(season, name = "snaps"), by = "season") |>
  transmute(Season = ifelse(season == current, paste0(sl(season), "$^\\ast$"), sl(season)),
            Teams = d1_teams, Ineligible = ineligible, `D-I games` = fmt(d1_played), `Non-D-I` = fmt(nond1_played),
            Eff. = pct(eff_share), Line = pct(line_share), Neutral = fmt(neutral), OT = fmt(ot), Snap. = snaps) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrrrr")
```

\vspace{-0.5em}
\qmdsmaller{$^\ast$ In progress. The first season is fitted once, at its end, to supply the next season's carry-over.}

# The Power Model {#sec-power}

## Likelihood {#sec-likelihood}

For game $g$ let
$$
\mu_g = r_{h(g),w(g)} - r_{a(g),w(g)} + \eta\,\delta_g
$$
be the expected regulation margin per 100 possessions: the difference between the two teams' strengths in the period of the game, plus the home-court advantage on the floor of whichever team is at home. Both observed signals depend on the teams only through $\mu_g$. How strengths move through the season is the subject of @sec-hierarchy.

A rate per 100 possessions is noisier when it is computed from fewer possessions: the margin of a 60-possession game varies more, per possession, than that of an 80-possession game. Each signal's variance is therefore divided by its game's weight, $\omega_g = n_g/70$ for the margin and $\omega^e_g = n^{\mathrm{live}}_g/70$ for the efficiency margin, so that the scales $\sigma_e$ and $\sigma_m$ refer to a game of 70 possessions.

::: {.defn label="Power model likelihood."}
For a game with an efficiency margin,
$$
e_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\lambda\mu_g,\ \sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g\bigr), \qquad
y_g \mid e_g, \mu_g \sim \mathcal{D}\bigl(\mu_g + \kappa(e_g - \lambda\mu_g),\ \sigma_m^2/\omega_g\bigr),
$$ {#eq-lik}
where $\mathcal{D}(\xi, \sigma^2)$ is a law with location $\xi$ and scale $\sigma$ from one of the families of @tbl-families. For a game without one,
$$
y_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{D}\bigl(\mu_g,\ \sigma_m^2/\omega_g + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g\bigr),
$$ {#eq-lik-marg}
with $\omega^e_g = 1$ when the live possessions are unknown. Games are conditionally independent given the parameters.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-families
#| tbl-cap: "The margin families. $t_\\nu(\\xi, \\sigma)$ is the Student-$t$ law with $\\nu$ degrees of freedom. The published family, chosen on out-of-sample predictions (@sec-family), is the normal."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Family, ~`$\\mathcal{D}(\\xi, \\sigma^2)$`, ~`Extra parameters`,
  "Normal (published)", "$\\mathcal{N}(\\xi, \\sigma^2)$", "none",
  "Student-$t$", "$t_\\nu(\\xi, \\sigma)$", "$\\nu$",
  "Contaminated normal", "$(1 - p_o)\\,\\mathcal{N}(\\xi, \\sigma^2) + p_o\\,\\mathcal{N}(\\xi, k_o^2\\sigma^2)$, $k_o > 1$", "$p_o, k_o$"
) |>
  ktab(align = "lll")
```

Three features of @eq-lik matter. First, both signals load on the same $\mu_g$, so strength is measured on the scale of the scoreboard margin: $\lambda$ converts it to the efficiency scale, and it is estimated. Second, the margin is modelled *given* the efficiency residual $e_g - \lambda\mu_g$. A team that shoots better than its expected efficiency usually outscores its expected margin too, and the loading $\kappa$ absorbs that shared component. Were the two modelled as conditionally independent given $\mu_g$, one good performance would be counted twice. Third, the noise is heteroscedastic in a known way, through the possession weights; beyond that, the family is a modelling choice made once, on out-of-sample predictions (@sec-family), and the published one is the normal: a margin is the sum of some seventy possessions each way, and heavier tails did not predict better.

The variance in @eq-lik-marg is chosen so that the two cases agree for the normal family.

::: {.thm label="Marginal Margin Lemma."}
Let $\mathcal{D}$ in @eq-lik be normal. Then, marginally over $e_g$, $y_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu_g, \sigma_m^2/\omega_g + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g\bigr)$, and $(e_g, y_g)$ is bivariate normal with mean $(\lambda\mu_g, \mu_g)$ and covariance
$$
\Sigma_g = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g & \kappa\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g \\ \kappa\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g & \sigma_m^2/\omega_g + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g \end{pmatrix}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $e_g = \lambda\mu_g + \varepsilon_e$ and $y_g = \mu_g + \kappa\varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_m$ with $\varepsilon_e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g)$ and $\varepsilon_m \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_m^2/\omega_g)$ independent. Then $(e_g, y_g)$ is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, with the stated mean, $\Var(y_g) = \kappa^2\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g + \sigma_m^2/\omega_g$ and $\Cov(e_g, y_g) = \kappa\sigma_e^2/\omega^e_g$.
:::

For the contaminated normal the same argument applies to each component of the mixture with the common scale inflated, and for the $t$ the marginal law of @eq-lik-marg is an approximation that matches the location and the scale; both matter only for the alternative families. At 70 possessions the marginal scale of the margin is $\bar\sigma = (\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2)^{1/2}$, `r fmt(median(final_full$sigma_game), 1)` points per 100 in a typical complete season, or about `r fmt(median(final_full$sigma_game) * 0.7, 1)` points per game. The same law defines the win probability.

::: {.defn label="Spread and win probability."}
For a game between teams $i$ and $j$ at site $v \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ from $i$'s side, with $\hat n$ expected possessions (@sec-tempo) and $\hat\omega = \hat n/70$, the predicted spread is the posterior mean of $\mu_{ij}(v)\,\hat n/100$, $\mu_{ij}^{(s)}(v) = r_i^{(s)} - r_j^{(s)} + \eta^{(s)} v$, and the win probability is
$$
p_{ij}(v) = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} \Phi\bigl(\mu_{ij}^{(s)}(v)\,\hat\omega^{1/2}/\bar\sigma^{(s)}\bigr).
$$
:::

This is the rule of @sternProbabilityWinningFootball1991 averaged over the posterior, which widens the predictive distribution by the uncertainty in the ratings, with one basketball-specific feature: a faster game is more predictable. The same difference in strength per 100 possessions translates into a larger expected margin over more possessions, while the noise of the margin grows only with their square root, so $p_{ij}$ moves away from one half as $\hat n$ grows. The ratings are those at the snapshot date; a game later in the week adds no drift.

## Hierarchy, Preseason Information and the Weekly Walk {#sec-hierarchy}

A team's strength starts the season at a preseason level, pooled within its conference, and then moves from period to period.

::: {.defn label="Strength hierarchy."}
For team $i$ in conference $c(i)$, the preseason level is
$$
r^0_i = \alpha_{c(i)} + \beta\, d_i + \beta_2\, d^{(2)}_i + \bigl(\tau^2 + \beta^2 s_i^2\bigr)^{1/2} z_i, \qquad
\alpha_c = \omega\, u_c, \qquad
z_i, u_c \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1).
$$ {#eq-hier}
Here $d_i$ is a preseason prediction of team $i$'s final rating on the scale of the model, $s_i$ the posterior standard deviation of its final rating last season (`r cfg$prior_sd_default` points when it has none), and $d^{(2)}_i$ its final rating two seasons back (zero when unknown).
:::

The prediction $d_i$ is the fitted value of a linear regression, fitted on every earlier season, of a team's final rating on its final rating the previous season, Torvik's preseason rating and the roster quantities of @sec-data. Where the regression has fewer than 300 team-seasons to learn from, in the first two seasons, $d_i$ is the even average of last season's rating and Torvik's preseason rating. The loading $\beta$ then measures how much of that prediction the season's games confirm, and is estimated jointly with everything else; with a well-calibrated prediction it should be near one. Because $d_i$ is a prediction of the rating itself, not of the deviation from the conference mean, it carries conference strength over as well, and the conference effects $\alpha_c$ absorb only what the prediction misses about a conference as a whole --- which is why their spread $\omega$ is small (@sec-priors).

::: {.defn label="Weekly random walk."}
Let $w_1 < w_2 < \cdots$ be the periods in which team $i$ plays, and $w_0 = 1/2$, the preseason level sitting half a period before the first. Its strength in those periods is
$$
r_{i,w_k} = r_{i,w_{k-1}} + \phi\,(w_k - w_{k-1})^{1/2}\,\varepsilon_{i,k}, \qquad r_{i,w_0} = r^0_i, \qquad \varepsilon_{i,k} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
$$ {#eq-walk}
so a team that does not play in a period accumulates that period's variance at its next game. Its rating at a snapshot date in period $w$ is its last state plus the drift since, $r_i = r_{i,w_K} + \phi\,(w - \tfrac12 - w_K)_+^{1/2}\varepsilon_i$.
:::

Only the periods in which a team plays carry a state, so a season adds about twenty parameters per team. The step $\phi$ is shared by all teams and estimated. It is the model's answer to how quickly a rating should forget: with $\phi = 0$ every game of the season counts equally, as in a static model, and the larger $\phi$ is relative to the noise of a game, the more the latest games dominate. @fig-tau shows the estimate by season: about `r fmt(median(final_full$tau), 2)` points per 100 per week, so over a twenty-week season a team's strength drifts by about `r fmt(median(final_full$tau) * sqrt(20), 1)` points (one sd), small next to the spread of Division I strengths but not next to the margin of a close game. Whether the drift improves predictions over static ratings is tested directly in @sec-ablation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tau
#| fig-cap: "Random-walk step $\\phi$ (left) and home-court advantage $\\eta$ (right) by season, per 100 possessions: posterior mean $\\pm 2$ sd of the full-season refit under vague priors (grey) and the published final posterior mean (orange). The dashed lines are the published prior means; the home-court prior of 2020--21 differs."
#| fig-scap: "Random-walk step and home court by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.34
vr <- refits |> filter(variable %in% c("tau", "hca")) |> select(season, variable, mean, sd)
pb <- final_full |> select(season, tau, hca) |> pivot_longer(-season, names_to = "variable", values_to = "pub")
lab2 <- c(tau = "phi~(step~per~week)", hca = "eta~(home~court)")
vr |> left_join(pb, by = c("season", "variable")) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(lab2[variable], levels = lab2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(season)) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(variable = factor(lab2, levels = lab2), pm = c(cfg$tau_prior[1], cfg$hca_prior[1])),
             aes(yintercept = pm), linetype = "dashed", colour = col_ref) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = mean - 2 * sd, ymax = mean + 2 * sd), colour = col_ref, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean), colour = col_ref, size = 1.4) +
  geom_point(aes(y = pub), colour = col_power, size = 1.8, shape = 18) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(first_season, last_full, 2), labels = \(x) sub("--", "-", sl(x), fixed = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per 100 possessions")
hca_s <- refits |> filter(variable == "hca")
```

The parameterisation is non-centred [@papaspiliopoulosGeneralFrameworkParametrization2007] throughout, in $z_i$, $u_c$ and the steps $\varepsilon_{i,k}$: in the first weeks each team has one or two games and the data barely constrain $z_i$, the regime in which a centred hierarchy produces the funnel geometry that defeats Hamiltonian samplers [@betancourtConceptualIntroductionHamiltonian2017]. The random walk has a funnel of its own, between $\phi$ and the steps, and one season identifies $\phi$ only weakly, which is why its prior is informative and keeps it away from zero (@sec-priors).

**Uncertainty in last season's rating.** The term $\beta^2 s_i^2$ in @eq-hier integrates out the uncertainty of last season's rating, treated as $\mathcal N(d_i, s_i^2)$: a team whose rating was poorly determined is shrunk further towards its conference. Using a posterior mean as the covariate is regression calibration [@carrollMeasurementErrorNonlinear2006], and since the posterior mean is already the best predictor of the true rating, the regression on it is not attenuated as a regression on a noisy measurement would be.

**One home-court advantage.** $\eta$ is one number per season for every home game. Arenas, crowds and travel surely differ [@harvilleHomeCourtAdvantageHow1994], and a team-specific home edge shrunk to the season's was tried and made no difference out of sample; the data identify one average well and many small effects poorly. @fig-tau shows the estimate by season: stable at about `r fmt(median(hca_s$mean[hca_s$season != 2021]), 1)` points per 100 possessions (`r fmt(median(hca_s$mean[hca_s$season != 2021]) * 0.7, 1)` points in a 70-possession game), except in `r sl(2021)`, played in empty or near-empty arenas, when it falls to `r fmt(hca_s$mean[hca_s$season == 2021], 1)`.

**Opponents outside Division I.** In a game against a team below Division I the Division I team's margin follows @eq-lik-marg with $\mu_g = r_{i,w(g)} - m_{\mathrm{nd}} + \eta\,\delta_g$ and an extra variance $\sigma_{\mathrm{nd}}^2$, one level $m_{\mathrm{nd}}$ for all such opponents. The spread $\sigma_{\mathrm{nd}}$ absorbs the difference between a good Division II team and an NAIA one. These games inform the Division I teams' strengths little --- they are mostly lopsided --- but they fill the early weeks, when a team may have played only one Division I game.

*Remark (identification).* The likelihood of Division I games depends on the strengths only through differences within a connected component of the schedule graph. Every prior in the model is proper, so the posterior is proper regardless, and the published ratings are centred, $\tilde r_i = r_i - \bar r$ over Division I teams, draw by draw: a rating of $+10$ means ten points per 100 possessions better than an average Division I team on a neutral floor. Between components the relative strengths come from the prior alone --- from the preseason prediction and the conference structure. In basketball that matters only in the first days of a season: `r { x <- sg |> group_by(season) |> filter(snap_date == min(snap_date[teams > 0])) |> ungroup(); paste0("at the first Monday the graph of teams that have played has ", fmt(min(x$components)), "--", fmt(max(x$components)), " components across seasons") }`, and from `r { x <- sg |> filter(components == 1) |> group_by(season) |> summarise(d = min(snap_date), f = min(sg$snap_date[sg$season == first(season) & sg$teams > 0])); paste0("the ", c("first", "second", "third", "fourth", "fifth", "sixth")[round(median(as.numeric(x$d - x$f) / 7 + 1))], " Monday in a typical season") }` it is connected.

@fig-dag draws the full model as a directed acyclic graph.

::: {#fig-dag fig-scap="The power model as a graphical model"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(r"(\begin{tikzpicture}[
  lat/.style={draw, circle, minimum size=0.95cm, inner sep=0pt, font=\small},
  obs/.style={lat, fill=gray!20},
  par/.style={font=\small, inner sep=2pt},
```

The power model. Shaded nodes are observed; plates repeat over conferences, teams (and, for $\varepsilon_{i,k}$ and $r_{i,w}$, the periods in which a team plays) and games; $s_i$, the uncertainty of $d_i$, enters $r^0_i$ alongside it and is not drawn, nor are the games against non-Division I opponents. The possessions $n_g$ set the weights of both signals. The efficiency margin $e_g$ is a parent of the scoreboard margin $y_g$, which is how the conditional likelihood of @eq-lik avoids counting one performance twice.
:::

## Tempo, Totals, Offence and Defence {#sec-tempo}

The power rating is per possession; a spread in points needs the number of possessions, and a total needs the points per possession as well. Both come from a model outside the Bayesian fit. Regulation possessions are regressed on a league mean and an additive effect for each team, and total points per 100 possessions (both teams) likewise, each a ridge regression --- a Gaussian random-effects model with the variance ratios fixed --- whose team effects shrink towards a fraction of last season's (`r TEMPO$carry_t` for tempo and `r TEMPO$carry_s` for scoring, the season-to-season regression slopes over the data), with games weighted by recency (half-life `r TEMPO$half_life` days) and points per 100 weighted by possessions. A game's expected possessions $\hat n$ are the sum of the mean and the two teams' tempo effects, and its expected total is $\hat n/100$ times the expected points per 100 plus a small allowance for overtime. With $t_i$ a team's scoring effect and $\bar x$ the league's points per 100, its **offence** and **defence** --- points scored and allowed per 100 possessions against an average team --- are
$$
\mathrm{Off}_i = \tfrac12 \bar x + \tfrac12(\tilde r_i + t_i), \qquad \mathrm{Def}_i = \tfrac12 \bar x + \tfrac12(t_i - \tilde r_i),
$$
so that $\mathrm{Off}_i - \mathrm{Def}_i = \tilde r_i$ by construction. The tempo model shares nothing with the power model, so it changes neither the power rating nor the resume, only the spreads, totals and the split into offence and defence. Its variance ratios and half-life were set on a weekly backtest of totals; it is scored against the closing over/under in @sec-bt-accuracy.

## Priors {#sec-priors}

```{r}
pp <- function(v) setNames(pooled$pooled_mean, pooled$variable)[[v]]
psd <- function(v) setNames(pooled$predictive_sd, pooled$variable)[[v]]
pool_used <- c(sigma_conf = "sigma_conf_prior", sigma_team = "sigma_team_prior", tau = "tau_prior", hca = "hca_prior")
pool_now <- map_dfr(names(pool_used), \(v) tibble(variable = v, cfg_mean = cfg[[pool_used[[v]]]][1], cfg_sd = cfg[[pool_used[[v]]]][2],
                                                  now_mean = pp(v), now_sd = psd(v)))
```

The hyperparameters of the hierarchy --- the spreads $\omega$ and $\tau$, the step $\phi$ and the home-court advantage $\eta$ --- describe the sport rather than any team. In the first weeks of a season, with a game or two per team, the data cannot estimate them, and with vague priors the sampler fails the convergence gates of @sec-gates. They are therefore given informative priors, set from history. Each complete season's final snapshot (about 5,500 games) is refitted under deliberately vague priors on every structural parameter (@sec-supp-justify); these refits are the `prior_refits` target of the pipeline. The season-by-season posterior means $\hat\theta_s$, with posterior standard deviations $v_s$, are then pooled by a random-effects meta-analysis [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013]. With the DerSimonian--Laird estimate $\hat\sigma_b^2$ of the between-season variance and weights $w_s = (v_s^2 + \hat\sigma_b^2)^{-1}$, each prior is centred at $\sum_s w_s\hat\theta_s / \sum_s w_s$ and its standard deviation is the predictive standard deviation for a new season,
$$
\sigma_{\text{prior}}^2 = \hat\sigma_b^2 + \Bigl(\sum_s w_s\Bigr)^{-1},
$$ {#eq-pool}
the season-to-season variation in excess of estimation noise plus the uncertainty of the centre, rounded up to the next 0.05 and to at least 0.1. Home court leaves out `r sl(2021)`, which has its own prior, $\mathcal N(`r cfg$hca_prior_season[["2021"]][1]`, `r cfg$hca_prior_season[["2021"]][2]`^2)$.

The other structural parameters --- the loadings $\beta$ and $\beta_2$, the scales and loadings of the two signals, and the non-Division I level --- are informed by thousands of games even in November, and get weakly informative priors on the scale of the sport. @tbl-priors lists every prior with the range of the full-season posterior means under the vague priors and as published.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-priors
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Priors (normal, truncated to the support where a parameter is constrained) and the range over complete seasons (", sl(first_season), " to ", sl(last_full), ") of the full-season posterior mean, refitted under vague priors and as published. The last column is the median posterior sd of the vague-prior refits. The first four are pooled from the refits (@eq-pool).")'
pri <- tibble::tribble(
  ~variable, ~field, ~what,
  "sigma_conf", "sigma_conf_prior", "conference spread",
  "sigma_team", "sigma_team_prior", "team spread",
  "tau", "tau_prior", "weekly step",
  "hca", "hca_prior", "home court (per 100)",
  "b_prev", "b_prev_prior", "loading of the preseason prediction",
  "b_prev2", "b_prev2_prior", "loading two seasons back",
  "lambda", "lambda_prior", "efficiency scale",
  "sigma_eff", "sigma_eff_prior", "efficiency noise",
  "kappa", "kappa_prior", "loading of the margin on it",
  "sigma_m", "sigma_m_prior", "margin noise",
  "r_nd_raw[1]", "r_nd_prior", "non-Division I level",
  "sigma_nd_raw[1]", "sigma_nd_prior", "its extra spread"
) |> mutate(mean = map_dbl(field, \(f) cfg[[f]][1]), sd = map_dbl(field, \(f) cfg[[f]][2]))
pub_final <- final_full |> select(season, any_of(pri$variable)) |>
  pivot_longer(-season, names_to = "variable") |>
  group_by(variable) |> summarise(plo = min(value), phi = max(value), .groups = "drop")
post <- refits |> filter(variable %in% pri$variable) |>
  group_by(variable) |> summarise(lo = min(mean), hi = max(mean), psd = median(sd), .groups = "drop")
pri |>
  left_join(post, by = "variable") |>
  left_join(pub_final, by = "variable") |>
  transmute(Parameter = paste(var_tex[variable], what),
            Prior = sprintf("$\\mathcal{N}(%s, %s^2)$", fmt(mean, 2), fmt(sd, 2)),
            `Vague priors` = sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(lo, 2), fmt(hi, 2)),
            Published = ifelse(is.na(plo), "--", sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(plo, 2), fmt(phi, 2))),
            `Post.\\ sd` = fmt(psd, 2)) |>
  ktab(align = "llrrr")
```

```{r}
noise_pars <- pooled |> filter(variable %in% pri$variable, between_sd < 1.3 * typical_post_sd) |> pull(variable)
pc <- pool_now |> mutate(z = abs(now_mean - cfg_mean) / cfg_sd)
```

The priors in use were pooled from an earlier run of the refits, under which only the four pooled scales had vague priors; the current refits, with every prior vague, pool to $\omega \sim \mathcal N(`r fmt(pp("sigma_conf"), 2)`, `r fmt(psd("sigma_conf"), 2)`^2)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal N(`r fmt(pp("sigma_team"), 2)`, `r fmt(psd("sigma_team"), 2)`^2)$, $\phi \sim \mathcal N(`r fmt(pp("tau"), 2)`, `r fmt(psd("tau"), 2)`^2)$ and $\eta \sim \mathcal N(`r fmt(pp("hca"), 2)`, `r fmt(psd("hca"), 2)`^2)$ before rounding. `r if (all(pc$z <= 0.5)) "Every published prior mean is within half a prior standard deviation of the current pooled mean." else paste0("The published prior means of ", sym_list(pc$variable[pc$z > 0.5]), " are more than half a prior standard deviation from the current pooled mean; the priors lag the refits by one rebuild, and @sec-supp-perturb shows how little the published ratings depend on them.")` The most consequential of the four is the conference spread: once the preseason prediction carries conference strength over, conference means move only about `r fmt(pp("sigma_conf"), 1)` points per 100 between seasons. For `r length(noise_pars)` of the `r nrow(pri)` parameters (`r sym_list(noise_pars)`) the between-season standard deviation of the posterior means is less than 1.3 times the typical within-season posterior standard deviation, about what sampling noise alone would produce: the history gives no evidence that these parameters change from season to season.

The priors are empirical Bayes at the level of the sport, and two consequences need checking. First, a season's own data help set its prior, so saying that its posterior lies inside that prior would be circular. @sec-supp-justify therefore also builds, for each season, the prior pooled from the *other* seasons only, and asks whether the season's own estimate lies inside it. Second, the early-season backtest of @sec-backtest for, say, `r sl(first_season + 1)` uses priors informed by later seasons. @sec-loso refits the first snapshots of every season under leave-one-season-out priors and measures the difference. @sec-supp-induced gives the priors they induce on team strengths, win probabilities and margins, and @sec-supp-perturb refits the model under widened and shifted priors.

# What the Efficiency Signal Adds {#sec-info}

The efficiency margin is expensive --- it needs play-by-play data, a shot model and every shooter's free-throw history --- and a natural question is how much it sharpens the estimate of strength once the scoreboard is known. The Gaussian version of the model answers it in closed form. Take a game of 70 possessions, $\omega_g = \omega^e_g = 1$; other lengths scale both informations by the same factor.

::: {.thm label="Information Proposition."}
In the Gaussian model of the Marginal Margin Lemma at unit weights, the Fisher information about $\mu_g$ carried by one game is
$$
\mathcal{I}_{y} = \frac{1}{\Sigma_{22}} = \frac{1}{\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2}
$$
from the margin alone, and
$$
\mathcal{I}_{e,y} = \frac{\lambda^2}{\sigma_e^2} + \frac{(1 - \kappa\lambda)^2}{\sigma_m^2}
= \mathcal{I}_y + \frac{(\lambda - \lambda^\ast)^2}{\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}},
\qquad \lambda^\ast = \frac{\Sigma_{12}}{\Sigma_{22}} = \frac{\kappa\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2},
$$ {#eq-info}
from both signals. Hence $\mathcal{I}_{e,y} \ge \mathcal{I}_y$, with equality exactly when $\lambda = \lambda^\ast$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For a Gaussian vector with mean $\bm a\mu$ and known covariance $\Sigma$ the information about $\mu$ is $\bm a^\top\Sigma^{-1}\bm a$. With $\bm a = (\lambda, 1)^\top$, factor the joint density as $p(y)\,p(e \mid y)$: the margin contributes $1/\Sigma_{22}$, and $e \mid y$ is normal with mean $\lambda\mu + (\Sigma_{12}/\Sigma_{22})(y - \mu)$ and variance $\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}$, whose derivative in $\mu$ is $\lambda - \lambda^\ast$. Adding the two informations gives the second form of @eq-info. The first form follows by factoring instead as $p(e)\,p(y \mid e)$: $e$ contributes $\lambda^2/\sigma_e^2$ and $y \mid e$ has mean $(1 - \kappa\lambda)\mu + \kappa e$ and variance $\sigma_m^2$.
:::

The proposition says that the efficiency margin helps exactly insofar as its scale $\lambda$ differs from $\lambda^\ast$, the slope of the regression of $e$ on $y$. If efficiency were nothing but a noisy copy of the scoreboard, its mean would move with $\mu$ exactly as the regression predicts from $y$, and it would add nothing. A luck-adjusted margin is not a noisy copy: by replacing the made threes and free throws by their expectations it removes the largest source of game-to-game noise from the scoreboard, so its residual variance is smaller, and its slope on strength is not the slope implied by its correlation with the margin.

```{r}
i25 <- info |> filter(season == last_full)
```

::: {.example}
At the end of `r sl(last_full)` the posterior means are $\lambda = `r fmt(i25$lambda, 3)`$, $\kappa = `r fmt(i25$kappa, 3)`$, $\sigma_e = `r fmt(i25$sigma_eff, 2)`$ and $\sigma_m = `r fmt(i25$sigma_m, 2)`$. The margin alone then has scale $\bar\sigma = `r fmt(sqrt(i25$S22), 2)`$ points per 100 and carries $\mathcal I_y = 1/\bar\sigma^2 = `r fmt(1000 * i25$i_y, 2)` \times 10^{-3}$ per game. The slope at which efficiency would add nothing is $\lambda^\ast = \kappa\sigma_e^2/\bar\sigma^2 = `r fmt(i25$lambda_star, 3)`$, `r fmt(abs(i25$lambda - i25$lambda_star), 3)` from the fitted $\lambda$, and both signals together carry $\mathcal I_{e,y} = `r fmt(1000 * i25$i_joint, 2)` \times 10^{-3}$: a gain of `r pct(i25$gain, 0)`, or about `r fmt(30 * i25$gain, 0)` extra games' worth of information over a thirty-game season.
:::

@tbl-info evaluates @eq-info at the posterior means of each complete season's final fit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-info
#| tbl-cap: "Per-game Fisher information about the expected margin per 100 possessions under the Gaussian model, at 70 possessions and each season's final posterior means. $R^2$ is the share of the margin's variance explained by the efficiency residual, $\\kappa^2\\sigma_e^2/\\bar\\sigma^2$."
info |>
  transmute(Season = sl(season), `$\\lambda$` = fmt(lambda, 3), `$\\lambda^\\ast$` = fmt(lambda_star, 3),
            `$R^2$` = fmt(r2, 2),
            `$10^3\\mathcal{I}_y$` = fmt(1000 * i_y, 2), `$10^3\\mathcal{I}_{e,y}$` = fmt(1000 * i_joint, 2),
            Gain = pct(gain, 0)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The efficiency residual explains `r pct(min(info$r2))`--`r pct(max(info$r2))` of the margin's variance, and the fitted $\lambda$ lies `r fmt(min(abs(info$lambda - info$lambda_star)), 2)`--`r fmt(max(abs(info$lambda - info$lambda_star)), 2)` from $\lambda^\ast$. The per-game information gain is `r pct(min(info$gain), 0)` to `r pct(max(info$gain), 0)`, about `r fmt(30 * min(info$gain), 0)`--`r fmt(30 * max(info$gain), 0)` extra games' worth over a thirty-game season. Two caveats limit how far this should be read. The calculation holds $\lambda$, $\kappa$ and the scales fixed, whereas in the fit they are estimated jointly with strength; and it is per game, at the posterior mean. The backtest is the arbiter. @sec-ablation refits the model without the efficiency likelihood at every snapshot of `r sl(min(abl_seasons))` to `r sl(max(abl_seasons))`: on the same `r fmt(abl_sum$games[abl_sum$variant == "Margin only"])` games, the margin-only model's mean absolute error is `r fmt(abs(abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$diff), 2)` points (standard error `r fmt(abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$se, 2)`) `r ifelse(abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$diff > 0, "higher", "lower")` and its log loss `r fmt(1000 * abs(abl_d("Margin only", "logloss")$diff), 1)` $\times 10^{-3}$ (se `r fmt(1000 * abl_d("Margin only", "logloss")$se, 1)`) `r ifelse(abl_d("Margin only", "logloss")$diff > 0, "higher", "lower")`. At each season's final posterior the expected log predictive density of the margin itself (@sec-loo) `r ifelse(median(cmp_eff$diff) > 0, "favours the full model", "favours the margin-only model")` by `r fmt(abs(median(cmp_eff$diff)), 0)` in a typical season (full minus margin-only: `r fmt(min(cmp_eff$diff), 0)` to `r fmt(max(cmp_eff$diff), 0)` across seasons, standard errors about `r fmt(median(cmp_eff$se), 0)`).

# The Resume {#sec-resume}

## Wins Above Bubble {#sec-wab}

A resume should value results, not performances, and should value them relative to a standard that matters for selection. The tournament takes `r field_size_now` teams, but not the `r field_size_now` best: each conference's champion qualifies automatically, however weak, and the committee chooses the rest. The natural standard for an at-large resume is therefore the last team to get in.

::: {.defn label="Bubble."}
In posterior draw $s$, let $A^{(s)}$ be the automatic bids --- each conference's tournament champion, or its regular-season leader where it holds no tournament; known once decided, and otherwise simulated in the draw (@sec-sim) --- and $E$ the teams eligible for the tournament. With a field of $F$ teams, the bubble strength $B^{(s)}$ is the $(F - |A^{(s)}|)$-th largest of $\{r_i^{(s)} : i \in E \setminus A^{(s)}\}$.
:::

The bubble is a strength, not a team: in different draws it is a different team, its uncertainty is part of the posterior, and so is the uncertainty in which conference champions remove themselves from the at-large pool. Since a weak champion takes a place without taking an at-large one, the bubble sits near the `r ord(median(params$bench_rank[params$kind == "selection" & params$season %in% complete]))`-best team by power in a typical season (the posterior mean rank of the bubble at Selection Monday), not the `r field_size_now`th.

::: {.defn label="Wins Above Bubble."}
Let team $i$ have played Division I games $g \in G_i$, with result $W_g \in \{0, 1\}$ (overtime wins count), opponent $o(g)$, site $v_g \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ from $i$'s side and possessions $n_g$. The probability that the bubble team would have won the same fixture is
$$
\pi_g^{(s)} = \Phi\Bigl(\bigl(B^{(s)} - r_{o(g)}^{(s)} + \eta^{(s)} v_g\bigr)\,\omega_g^{1/2} / \bar\sigma^{(s)}\Bigr),
$$
the win probability of @sec-likelihood with the bubble in team $i$'s place, and
$$
\WAB_i^{(s)} = \sum_{g \in G_i}\bigl(W_g - \pi_g^{(s)}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-wab}
The published value is the posterior mean $\WAB_i = S^{-1}\sum_s \WAB_i^{(s)}$ with an 80\% interval.
:::

@eq-wab uses the scoreboard only through $W_g$: margin enters the resume solely by having informed the strengths of the opponents and the bubble. Both are taken at the date of the snapshot, not at the date of the game: an opponent is valued at what the posterior now believes it to be, so a November win over a team that improves gains value as it does. The following properties are elementary but they are the reason for the choice.

::: {.thm label="WAB Properties."}
For every draw $s$:

(i) *Additivity.* $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ is a sum of per-game contributions $W_g - \pi_g^{(s)}$, each in $(-1, 1)$.
(ii) *Monotonicity.* A win contributes $1 - \pi_g^{(s)} > 0$ and a loss $-\pi_g^{(s)} < 0$; with the draw held fixed, changing any loss to a win raises $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ by exactly one, whatever the opponent.
(iii) *Schedule response.* The contribution of a win is increasing in the opponent's strength and that of a loss is increasing too (a loss to a strong team costs less), and both are decreasing in the site $v_g$: road wins count for more than home wins.
(iv) *Calibration.* If the model is correct and team $i$ has strength $r_i^{(s)} = B^{(s)}$, then $\E[\WAB_i^{(s)} \mid \text{parameters}] = 0$ for every schedule.
:::

::: {.proof}
Parts (i) and (ii) are immediate from @eq-wab, since $0 < \pi_g^{(s)} < 1$. For (iii), $\pi_g^{(s)}$ is decreasing in $r_{o(g)}$ and increasing in $v_g$, and both contributions have the form $\text{const} - \pi_g^{(s)}$. For (iv), under the model $\Pr(W_g = 1) = \Phi\bigl((r_i - r_{o(g)} + \eta v_g)\,\omega_g^{1/2}/\bar\sigma\bigr) = \pi_g^{(s)}$ when $r_i = B^{(s)}$; an overtime game, a regulation tie, is decided by a coin flip of equal teams in the model's terms, which leaves the expectation unchanged when the teams are equal and moves it little otherwise.
:::

Property (ii) holds draw by draw. The *published* $\WAB_i$ changes by a slightly different amount when a result flips, because the result is also data for the posterior: a win moves the opponent's strength down, and the bubble with it. @sec-leakage measures a related effect of the margin. Property (ii) excludes what a strength-of-schedule bonus does, rewarding a team for *playing* strong opponents regardless of result; (iii) is the precise sense in which the schedule is counted once; and (iv) gives the scale its meaning: a positive $\WAB$ is evidence of having done better than a bubble team would have with the same games. Summing over games makes $\WAB$ a count, not a rate, so a team that wins an extra game in a conference tournament gains from it. That is intended: every game is a chance to earn or lose standing, and the committee sees the same games.

The possession weight in $\pi_g$ is the only place where the margin's scale enters the resume, and it enters as the model's estimate of how decisive a game of that length is, not through the game's own result.

```{r}
# The bubble at Selection Monday of the last complete season: the last at-large team by our WAB,
# from the Selection Monday refit's per-game rows (posterior means of the bubble's chances)
sl_last <- Filter(\(x) x$season == last_full, selr)[[1]]
fld <- sl_last$field
b0_last <- sel_bench |> filter(season == last_full, benchmark == "Last team in (published)", pool) |> arrange(desc(wab))
n_al_last <- sum(!fld$auto)
bubble <- sel_last |> filter(team_id == b0_last$team_id[n_al_last])
first_out <- sel_last |> filter(team_id == b0_last$team_id[n_al_last + 1])
team_name <- function(id) board$team[match(id, board$team_id)]
bub_games <- sl_last$games |> filter(team_id == bubble$team_id) |>
  arrange(game_date) |>
  mutate(opp = team_name(opp_id), venue = c("A", "N", "H")[venue + 2], cum = cumsum(win - p_bench))
sor_bub <- { dist <- 1; for (p in bub_games$p_bench) dist <- c(dist * (1 - p), 0) + c(0, dist * p); sum(dist[(sum(bub_games$win) + 1):length(dist)]) }
```

::: {.example}
@tbl-wab-example works through $\WAB$ for `r esc(bubble$team)`, `r bubble$wins`--`r bubble$losses` at Selection Monday of `r sl(last_full)` and the last of the `r n_al_last` at-large teams by $\WAB$, given the actual automatic bids; `r esc(first_out$team)` was the first team out. For each game, $\bar\pi_g$ is the posterior mean probability that the bubble team would have won the same fixture at the same site; the contribution is $W_g - \bar\pi_g$, and $\WAB$ is their sum, `r fmt(sum(bub_games$win - bub_games$p_bench), 2)` in this refit (the published value, from a separate fit, is `r fmt(bubble$wab, 2)`). `r esc(bubble$team)` was `r if (bubble$team_id %in% fld$team_id) paste0("in the committee's field, as ", if (fld$seed[fld$team_id == bubble$team_id] %in% c(8, 11, 18)) "an " else "a ", fld$seed[fld$team_id == bubble$team_id], " seed") else "not in the committee's field"`.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wab-example
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Wins Above Bubble, game by game, for ", esc(bubble$team), " at Selection Monday of ", sl(last_full), ". H, A, N: home, away, neutral. $\\bar\\pi_g$: probability that the bubble team would win the same fixture.")'
bub_games |>
  transmute(Date = format(game_date, "%b %d"), Opponent = esc(opp), Site = venue,
            Score = paste0(pts_for, "--", pts_against), `$W_g$` = win, `$\\bar\\pi_g$` = fmt(p_bench, 3),
            `$W_g - \\bar\\pi_g$` = fmt(win - p_bench, 3), `Running $\\WAB$` = fmt(cum, 2)) |>
  ktab(align = "lllrrrrr")
```

## The Rest of the Season {#sec-sim}

Before the automatic bids are decided, the bubble depends on who will win them. In each posterior draw the rest of the season is therefore played out: the remaining regular-season games from the draw's ratings and home court, then each conference tournament as a single-elimination bracket of the size the conference used the previous season, seeded by the simulated standings, with byes for the top seeds; a champion already crowned is fixed, as is the standings leader of a conference without a tournament. A champion still moving up to Division I is ineligible and the bid passes to the best eligible team in the standings, as those conferences did. The simulated champions are the draw's automatic bids, which set its bubble, and the draw's projected $\WAB$ --- $\WAB$ so far plus the simulated games, each scored against the same bubble --- picks the at-large teams among the rest. The published probabilities of an automatic bid, an at-large bid and a place in the field come out jointly, and sum correctly over teams in every draw. The simulation uses the same draws as the resume, so its uncertainty is the posterior's; it does not simulate the selection committee, only a committee that selects by projected $\WAB$.

## Strength of Record, Quadrants and Ranks {#sec-sor}

Three further quantities are reported with the resume, as on the committee's team sheets. The **strength of record** is the probability that a top-25 team would do at least as well as team $i$ did against its schedule: $\SOR_i = \Pr\bigl(\sum_{g} T_g \ge \sum_{g} W_g\bigr)$ with independent $T_g \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\bar\pi^{25}_g)$, where $\bar\pi^{25}_g$ is the posterior mean probability that the draw's 25th-best team wins game $g$'s fixture. The sum of independent Bernoulli variables with unequal probabilities is Poisson-binomial, and its distribution is computed exactly by the recursion
$$
P_0^{(0)} = 1, \qquad
P_k^{(t)} = (1 - \bar\pi_t)P_k^{(t-1)} + \bar\pi_t P_{k-1}^{(t-1)}, \quad k = 0, \ldots, t,
$$
over a team's games [@hongComputingDistributionFunction2013]. Smaller is more impressive. **Quadrant records** count wins and losses against opponents grouped by their power rank and the site, with the cut-offs the committee uses for its own ranking (top 30 at home, 50 neutral, 75 away for the first quadrant, and so on), applied to our ranks. **Schedule strength** is the bubble team's expected loss rate against the schedule, $1 - |G_i|^{-1}\sum_g \bar\pi_g$.

$\SOR$ plugs in the posterior mean $\bar\pi^{25}_g$ rather than averaging the per-draw probabilities as $\WAB$ does, and the two differ because the tail probability is non-linear in $\pi_g$. Refitting each Selection Monday with every draw kept, the largest difference over all teams and seasons is `r fmt(max(sor_cmp$max_diff), 3)` and the rank correlation of the two versions is at least `r fmt(min(sor_cmp$rho), 3)`, so the cheaper version loses nothing.

Uncertainty in ranks is reported by ranking within each draw.

::: {.defn label="Posterior rank summaries."}
Let $R_i^{(s)}$ be the rank of $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ among Division I teams in draw $s$ (1 is best). The published rank orders the posterior means $\WAB_i$, and the 80\% rank interval is the 10\% and 90\% quantiles of $\{R_i^{(s)}\}_s$. The power rank is defined in the same way from $\tilde r_i^{(s)}$.
:::

The published rank orders posterior means rather than taking the median rank, because the median ranks of different teams need not form a permutation.

## Record-only Reference: the Colley Matrix {#sec-colley}

The model's resume uses opponent strengths from a model that sees margins. As a reference that sees only wins and losses we compute the Colley rating [@colleyColleysBiasFree2002; @langvilleWhosNumberOne2012].

::: {.defn label="Colley rating."}
Let $n_i$ be team $i$'s games, $w_i$ and $l_i$ its wins and losses, and $n_{ij}$ the number of games between $i$ and $j$. The Colley ratings $\bm c$ solve $C\bm c = \bm f$ with
$$
C_{ii} = 2 + n_i, \qquad C_{ij} = -n_{ij} \ (i \ne j), \qquad f_i = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}(w_i - l_i).
$$
:::

::: {.thm label="Colley Lemma."}
$C$ is symmetric positive definite, so $\bm c$ exists and is unique, and $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i c_i = \frac{1}{2}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$C = 2I + L$, where $L$ is the Laplacian of the schedule multigraph, which is positive semidefinite; so $C$ is positive definite. Every column of $L$ sums to zero, so $\bm 1^\top C = 2\bm 1^\top$ and $2\,\bm 1^\top\bm c = \bm 1^\top C\bm c = \bm 1^\top\bm f = n + \frac{1}{2}\sum_i(w_i - l_i) = n$, since every game produces one win and one loss.
:::

The rating is Laplace's rule of succession, $(1 + w_i)/(2 + n_i)$, adjusted for the average rating of the opponents. We compute it on the same Division I games as the posterior; it ignores site, so a home win counts as much as a road win.

## Choosing the Benchmark {#sec-bench}

The bubble is a choice about what the resume is for, not a parameter that data could estimate: a resume is retrodictive, and there is no future outcome against which a backtest could score it. It answers the question the committee answers for at-large teams --- would a team on the edge of the field have done this well? --- and two features of its construction follow from that question rather than from convenience: it removes the automatic bids before counting, and it uses the field's size, not a fixed rank. @tbl-bench shows how much the choice matters, by recomputing $\WAB$ at Selection Monday of every complete season with tournament under four alternatives: the bubble moved four places up or down the at-large order, and two benchmarks that ignore the bids, the 45th and the 25th-best team by power. The last column counts how many of the committee's at-large teams each benchmark's top $\WAB$ would have selected, given the actual automatic bids.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bench
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the Selection Monday resume to the benchmark, over complete seasons with a tournament. Rank correlation of $\\WAB$ with the published bubble, among all Division I teams; the number of at-large selections by $\\WAB$ that change; the mean posterior power rank of the benchmark; and the at-large teams the committee also chose (mean over seasons, of the number of at-large places). Median over seasons, with the range."
rng <- function(x, d = 0) sprintf("%s (%s--%s)", fmt(median(x), d), fmt(min(x), d), fmt(max(x), d))
bench_tab <- bind_rows(
  bench_pub |> transmute(benchmark = "Last team in (published)", rho = 1, pick_changes = 0, bench_rank, overlap, at_large),
  bench_cmp |> left_join(bench_pub |> select(season, at_large), by = "season") |>
    transmute(benchmark, rho, pick_changes, bench_rank, overlap, at_large)
) |>
  group_by(benchmark) |>
  summarise(rho = if (benchmark[1] == "Last team in (published)") "--" else rng(rho, 3),
            changes = if (benchmark[1] == "Last team in (published)") "--" else rng(pick_changes),
            br = fmt(mean(bench_rank), 0), ov = sprintf("%s of %s", fmt(mean(overlap), 1), fmt(mean(at_large), 1)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(benchmark = factor(benchmark, levels = names(c("Last team in (published)" = 1, "Last four byes" = 1, "First four out" = 1,
                                                          "Power rank 45" = 1, "Power rank 25" = 1)))) |>
  arrange(benchmark)
bench_tab |>
  transmute(Benchmark = as.character(benchmark), `$\\rho$ with published` = rho, `At-large picks changed` = changes,
            `Benchmark rank` = br, `Committee's at-large picked` = ov) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrr")
bm <- function(b, col) bench_cmp |> filter(benchmark == b) |> pull(col)
```

Over the whole of Division I the order barely depends on the benchmark (median rank correlation at least `r fmt(min(map_dbl(unique(bench_cmp$benchmark), \(b) median(bm(b, "rho")))), 3)`), because a benchmark changes the price of each result but not which results are good. The edge of the field does move: a stronger benchmark makes a loss cheap and a win over a weak team nearly worthless, which favours difficult schedules, while a weaker one makes every win count and every loss costly. Moving the bubble four places changes `r { m <- max(c(bm("First four out", "pick_changes"), bm("Last four byes", "pick_changes"))); if (m == 0) "none of the at-large selections in any season" else paste0("at most ", m, " of the at-large selections in any season, and ", if (median(c(bm("First four out", "pick_changes"), bm("Last four byes", "pick_changes"))) == 0) "none" else "few", " in a typical one") }`. The 45th-best team by power, which ignores the bids, sits close to the published bubble in rank and `r { m <- max(bm("Power rank 45", "pick_changes")); if (m == 0) "selects the same at-large teams in every season" else paste0("changes at most ", m, " at-large selection", if (m > 1) "s" else "", " a season") }`; only the 25th-best team, a much stronger benchmark, moves the edge of the field. Which benchmark agrees best with the committee is a question about the committee, not about the measure; @sec-validate-resume compares the published one with its choices.

## How Margin Reaches the Resume {#sec-leakage}

$\WAB$ does not use margin directly, but margin informs the posterior strengths of the opponents and the bubble, so it reaches the resume indirectly. A blowout win makes the loser look weaker, which lowers the winner's credit for beating it. @tbl-leakage measures this on the `r nrow(leak) / 2` most lopsided Division I games of `r sl(last_full)`: each is refitted at the final snapshot with its regulation margin replaced by a one-point win for the same team (and its efficiency margin dropped), and the two teams' $\WAB$ and power ratings recomputed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-leakage
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Effect of a blowout margin on the resume, ", sl(last_full), " final posterior. For each game: the change in each team''s $\\WAB$ and power rating (per 100 possessions) when the result is refitted as a one-point win for the same team, and the mean absolute change in $\\WAB$ of every other team.")'
leak |>
  mutate(d_wab = wab_new - wab_base, d_pow = power_new - power_base) |>
  group_by(game_id) |>
  summarise(Game = paste0(esc(team[role == "winner"]), " over ", esc(team[role == "loser"])),
            Margin = margin[1],
            `$\\Delta\\WAB$ winner` = fmt(d_wab[role == "winner"], 3),
            `$\\Delta\\WAB$ loser` = fmt(d_wab[role == "loser"], 3),
            `$\\Delta$ power winner` = fmt(d_pow[role == "winner"], 1),
            `$\\Delta$ power loser` = fmt(d_pow[role == "loser"], 1),
```
