```{r}
            Others = fmt(others_wab[1], 3), .groups = "drop") |>
  select(-game_id) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
leak_w <- leak |> filter(role == "winner") |> mutate(d = wab_new - wab_base)
leak_l <- leak |> filter(role == "loser") |> mutate(d = wab_new - wab_base)
```

Turning a blowout of `r fmt(min(leak$margin))`--`r fmt(max(leak$margin))` points into a one-point win moves the winner's power rating by `r fmt(min(abs(leak_w$power_new - leak_w$power_base)), 1)`--`r fmt(max(abs(leak_w$power_new - leak_w$power_base)), 1)` points per 100, but its $\WAB$ by `r fmt(min(leak_w$d), 3)` to `r fmt(max(leak_w$d), 3)` wins and the loser's by `r fmt(min(leak_l$d), 3)` to `r fmt(max(leak_l$d), 3)`; every other team's moves by at most `r fmt(max(leak$others_wab), 3)` on average. For comparison, the Monte Carlo standard error of a published $\WAB$ is about `r fmt(median(mcse_all$wab_mcse, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` (@sec-gates). The margin's influence on the resume runs through the opponents' strengths, as designed, and a team gains little by running up a score. Most of these games are against the weakest teams in Division I, whose strength barely matters to anyone's resume.

# Computation and Pipeline {#sec-computation}

## Sampling and Gates {#sec-gates}

Each posterior is sampled with the No-U-Turn sampler [@hoffmanNoUTurnSampler2014] in Stan [@carpenterStanProbabilisticProgramming2017] via CmdStan: `r cfg$chains` chains of `r fmt(cfg$warmup)` warm-up and `r fmt(cfg$sampling)` sampling iterations, target acceptance `r cfg$adapt_delta`. A fit is checked against four gates on every team's centred rating at the snapshot date and every structural parameter: rank-normalised $\widehat{R} \le 1.01$ and bulk effective sample size of at least 400 [@vehtariRankNormalizationFoldingLocalization2021], no divergent transitions, and E-BFMI above 0.2 in every chain [@betancourtConceptualIntroductionHamiltonian2017]. A snapshot that fails is still published, with the failure recorded; the informative priors of @sec-priors were adopted precisely because they make failures rare. The resume, the team sheet and the season simulation use all `r fmt(cfg$chains * cfg$sampling)` draws. @tbl-mcse measures what that buys, from the Selection Monday refits of every complete season: the Monte Carlo standard errors of the published quantities.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mcse
#| tbl-cap: "Monte Carlo standard errors of published quantities at Selection Monday, all Division I teams of every complete season with a tournament: median and largest over teams and seasons, with every post-warm-up draw."
mcse_all |>
  summarise(across(c(rating_mcse, wab_mcse, p_pos_mcse, rank_q10_mcse, rank_q90_mcse),
                   \(x) sprintf("%s / %s", fmt(median(x, na.rm = TRUE), 3), fmt(max(x, na.rm = TRUE), 3)))) |>
  transmute(`Power rating` = rating_mcse, `$\\WAB$` = wab_mcse, `$\\Pr(\\WAB > 0)$` = p_pos_mcse,
            `Rank, 10\\% quantile` = rank_q10_mcse, `Rank, 90\\% quantile` = rank_q90_mcse) |>
  ktab(align = "rrrrr")
```

The largest Monte Carlo error of a published $\WAB$ is `r fmt(max(mcse_all$wab_mcse, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` wins, and of a rating `r fmt(max(mcse_all$rating_mcse, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` points per 100: small next to the posterior uncertainty they summarise, so the second decimal of a published $\WAB$ is meaningful and the third is not.

Of the `r fmt(n_snap)` posteriors, `r fmt(n_pass)` pass every gate. @tbl-gates summarises them by season.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gates
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence gates by season, over all snapshots. Worst values are taken over snapshots and over every monitored parameter; \\emph{Minutes} is total sampling time, four chains in parallel."
fit_snaps |>
  group_by(Season = sl(season)) |>
  summarise(Snapshots = n(), Passed = sum(pass),
            `Max $\\widehat R$` = fmt(max(max_rhat), 3),
            `Min ESS` = fmt(min(min_ess)),
            Divergent = sum(divergences),
            `Min E-BFMI` = fmt(min(min_ebfmi), 2),
            Minutes = fmt(sum(secs) / 60, 0)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrr")
fails <- fit_snaps |> filter(!pass)
```

`r if (nrow(fails)) paste0("The ", nrow(fails), " failures are all of one kind: ", if (all(fails$divergences == 0)) "no divergences, " else "", "the smallest effective sample size or largest $\\widehat R$ belongs to ", paste(ifelse(unique(fails$worst) %in% names(var_tex), var_tex[unique(fails$worst)], paste0("\\texttt{", gsub("_", "\\\\_", unique(fails$worst)), "}")), collapse = " or "), ", with $\\widehat R$ at most ", fmt(max(fails$max_rhat), 3), " and effective sample size at least ", fmt(min(fails$min_ess)), ": slow mixing of a weakly identified scale, not a failure of the sampler to explore, and too small to move a published rating.") else "Every snapshot passes."`

## The Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

The computation is a `targets` pipeline in R [@landauTargetsPackageDynamic2021; @rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2026], drawn in @fig-pipeline. Its structure enforces the two properties the evaluation depends on. First, the input to a snapshot contains only games played before its date, and the schedule of later games without their results, and is hashed, so a cached posterior is reused exactly when its input is unchanged, and new results or betting lines never invalidate it. Second, each season's preseason information is the final posterior of the previous season, and the roster regression is fitted on the seasons before; the pipeline tracks both dependencies, so refitting one season refits every later one. The shot model of a season is trained on the two seasons before it, for the same reason. The analyses of this paper are targets too, built on request; they read the published inputs and never write to them.

::: {#fig-pipeline fig-scap="The targets pipeline"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(r"(\begin{tikzpicture}[
  box/.style={draw, rounded corners=2pt, align=center, font=\small,
              inner sep=4pt, minimum height=0.9cm, fill=white},
  store/.style={box, fill=gray!12},
  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]}, thick},
  node distance=0.45cm and 0.55cm]
\node[store, text width=2.4cm] (api) {ESPN bulk files, CBBD, Torvik};
\node[store, text width=2.1cm, right=of api] (raw) {raw cache\\\scriptsize files, JSON};
\node[store, text width=2.1cm, right=of raw] (db) {DuckDB\\\scriptsize games, shots, lines, rosters};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, below=1.1cm of db] (data) {\texttt{games\_}$s$\\\scriptsize signals, venues};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of data] (shot) {\texttt{shotmodel\_}$s$\\\scriptsize trained on $s{-}2, s{-}1$};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of shot] (prior) {\texttt{prior\_}$s$\\\scriptsize final of $s{-}1$, Torvik, roster};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, below=1.1cm of shot] (inputs) {\texttt{inputs\_}$s$[$d$]\\\scriptsize games before $d$};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of inputs] (dates) {\texttt{dates\_}$s$\\\scriptsize opening, Mondays, final};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, right=of inputs] (snaps) {\texttt{snaps\_}$s$[$d$]\\\scriptsize NUTS, ratings, resume, simulation};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, below=1.1cm of inputs] (all) {\texttt{snapshots}\\\scriptsize + polls};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, right=of all] (bt) {\texttt{backtest}\\\scriptsize $d$ predicts until next};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of all] (paper) {analyses, this paper\\\scriptsize \texttt{CBB\_PAPER=1}};
\draw[arr] (api) -- (raw); \draw[arr] (raw) -- (db); \draw[arr] (db) -- (data);
\draw[arr] (shot) -- (data);
\draw[arr] (data) -- (inputs); \draw[arr] (prior) -- (inputs); \draw[arr] (dates) -- (inputs);
\draw[arr] (inputs) -- (snaps); \draw[arr] (snaps) -- (all); \draw[arr] (all) -- (bt);
\draw[arr] (all) -- (paper);
\draw[arr, dashed] (snaps.north) to[out=90, in=0] node[above, font=\scriptsize, pos=0.3] {final of $s$ $\to$ $s{+}1$} (prior.north east);
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=south] at (inputs.north) {map over dates $d$};
\end{tikzpicture})")
```

The computation as a `targets` pipeline. Grey boxes are external stores; white boxes are targets, with $[d]$ marking a dynamic branch per snapshot date and $s$ a season. The dashed edge is the only cross-season dependency of the published fits: season $s$'s final ratings become season $s+1$'s preseason information. In season, a daily build fetches the new results and refits only the latest snapshot.
:::

# Model Checking {#sec-checks}

Each complete season's final posterior is refitted with the pointwise log-likelihood stored, and three checks are run on it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gabryVisualizationBayesianWorkflow2019]. This section summarises them across seasons; @sec-supp examines two posteriors in full detail --- sampler diagnostics, convergence, posterior geometry, prior-to-posterior learning, predictive distributions and influence.

## Posterior Predictive Checks {#sec-ppc}

Replicated regulation margins per 100 possessions are drawn from @eq-lik-marg, each game at its expected margin in the period it was played, turned into points with the game's regulation possessions and rounded to whole points, so that they can land exactly on the thresholds of the statistics. They are compared with six observed statistics: the standard deviation of the margin in points, the shares of games within three and within ten points, the share decided by 20 or more, the share tied after regulation, and the home team's regulation win rate on its own floor; the efficiency margin is compared on its standard deviation. @fig-ppc shows the result for every season.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive checks at each complete season's final posterior. Bars: central 90\\% interval of the statistic over 400 replicated seasons; points: the observed value, filled when it falls outside the interval."
#| fig-scap: "Posterior predictive checks by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.85
ppc_all |>
  mutate(outside = observed < rep_lo | observed > rep_hi,
         statistic = factor(statistic, levels = unique(statistic))) |>
  ggplot(aes(season)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = rep_lo, ymax = rep_hi), colour = col_ref, linewidth = 2.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed, shape = outside), colour = col_ink, size = 1.6, fill = "white") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 21, `TRUE` = 19), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~statistic, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(28)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(first_season, last_full, 4), labels = \(x) sub("--", "-", sl(x), fixed = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
ppc_out <- ppc_all |> group_by(statistic) |>
  summarise(out = sum(observed < rep_lo | observed > rep_hi), above = sum(observed > rep_hi),
            below = sum(observed < rep_lo), n = n(), lo = min(observed), hi = max(observed),
            rlo = min(rep_mean), rhi = max(rep_mean), .groups = "drop")
po <- function(s, col = "out") ppc_out[[col]][ppc_out$statistic == s]
fit_ok <- ppc_out |> filter(out <= 1) |> pull(statistic)
fit_bad <- ppc_out |> filter(out > 1)
```

`r if (length(fit_ok)) paste0("The model reproduces ", knitr::combine_words(tolower(sub(" [(].*", "", fit_ok))), " (outside the interval in at most one season each). ") else ""``r if (nrow(fit_bad)) paste0("It misses ", knitr::combine_words(paste0(tolower(fit_bad$statistic), " in ", fit_bad$out, " of ", fit_bad$n, " seasons (observed ", fmt(fit_bad$lo, 3), "--", fmt(fit_bad$hi, 3), ", replicated mean ", fmt(fit_bad$rlo, 3), "--", fmt(fit_bad$rhi, 3), ")")), ".") else ""` The share tied after regulation is the clearest case: a continuous law around the rating difference gives a tie only when a replicate rounds to zero, while real games are tied at the end of regulation more often, because the end of a close game is played to the score --- the trailing team fouls and shoots threes to tie, the leading team plays for the last shot. These ties are the overtime games, whose regulation margin is zero by construction. The misfit is in the *shape* of the margin distribution near zero; the win probabilities, which depend on the location and the scale, are well calibrated (@sec-backtest).

## Prior Sensitivity {#sec-sens}

Power-scaling sensitivity [@kallioinenDetectingDiagnosingPrior2024] perturbs the prior and the likelihood by raising each to a power near one, estimates the resulting change in each marginal posterior by importance sampling, and flags a parameter whose posterior moves under both (prior--data conflict) or under the prior alone (weak likelihood). The likelihood here is that of the Division I games, efficiency and margin together. @tbl-sens counts the flags across seasons.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens
#| tbl-cap: "Power-scaling sensitivity by parameter, at each complete season's final posterior. Sensitivities are the cumulative Jensen--Shannon distance between the base and the power-scaled posteriors; the conventional threshold is 0.05."
flag_counts |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = intersect(names(sym_lab), variable))) |>
  arrange(variable) |>
  transmute(Parameter = var_tex[as.character(variable)], `Prior (median)` = fmt(prior, 3),
            `Likelihood (median)` = fmt(likelihood, 3),
            `Seasons flagged: conflict` = paste0(conflict, "/", n),
            `weak likelihood` = paste0(weak, "/", n)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrr")
fc_conf <- flag_counts |> filter(conflict > 0)
fc_weak <- flag_counts |> filter(weak > 0)
pooled_vars <- c("sigma_conf", "sigma_team", "tau", "hca")
```

`r if (nrow(fc_weak)) nrow(fc_weak) else "None"` of the `r nrow(flag_counts)` parameters `r if (nrow(fc_weak) == 1) "is" else "are"` flagged for a weak likelihood in any season`r if (nrow(fc_weak)) paste0(" (", sym_list(fc_weak$variable), ")") else ""`, and `r nrow(fc_conf)` for prior--data conflict in at least one`r if (nrow(fc_conf)) paste0(" (", sym_list(fc_conf$variable), ")") else ""`. The game-level parameters --- the scales and loadings of the two signals --- are set by thousands of games and their priors do not matter. The flags fall on the parameters that one season identifies only weakly: the hierarchy's spreads, the step, home court and the preseason loadings. For the four pooled ones that is what the pooling of @sec-priors produces, and not a sign that the seasons disagree with their history: each pooled prior carries the information of a dozen seasons (@eq-pool), so its standard deviation is comparable to or smaller than that of a single season's full-data posterior, and power-scaling either the prior or the likelihood then moves the posterior; priorsense labels a parameter that is sensitive to both a conflict. Whether a season actually departs from its prior is answered directly by the leave-one-season-out column of @tbl-supp-justify. How much the priors move the published products themselves is the subject of @sec-supp-perturb.

## Leave-one-out Cross-validation {#sec-loo}

Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [@vehtariPracticalBayesianModel2017; @vehtariParetoSmoothedImportance2024] estimates the expected log predictive density of a new game, with the Pareto $\hat k$ diagnostic flagging games whose removal would change the posterior too much for the approximation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo
#| tbl-cap: "PSIS-LOO at each complete season's final posterior, on each Division I game's joint density of efficiency and margin. $p_{\\mathrm{loo}}$ is the effective number of parameters; the last column counts games with $\\hat k > 0.7$."
n_teams_s <- cov |> select(season, teams = d1_teams)
loo_tab <- loo_tab |> left_join(n_teams_s, by = "season")
loo_tab |>
  transmute(Season = sl(season), Games = fmt(games), Teams = teams,
            `$\\widehat{\\mathrm{elpd}}_{\\mathrm{loo}}$` = fmt(elpd, 0), SE = fmt(se, 0),
            `$p_{\\mathrm{loo}}$` = fmt(p_loo, 0), `$\\hat k > 0.7$` = bad_k) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The effective number of parameters is `r fmt(min(loo_tab$p_loo), 0)`--`r fmt(max(loo_tab$p_loo), 0)`, `r fmt(min(loo_tab$p_loo / loo_tab$teams), 1)`--`r fmt(max(loo_tab$p_loo / loo_tab$teams), 1)` per team: a team's strength is a level and a walk of some twenty states, which the random walk and the hierarchy shrink heavily. `r if (max(loo_tab$bad_k) == 0) "No game has $\\hat k > 0.7$ in any season" else paste0("At most ", max(loo_tab$bad_k), if (max(loo_tab$bad_k) == 1) " game per season has" else " games per season have", " $\\hat k > 0.7$")`: with thirty games per team no single game determines a team's strength. Because `log_lik` is the joint density of both signals where efficiency is observed, its $\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}$ cannot be compared with that of a model without efficiency; the program therefore also stores the marginal density of the margin alone, on which @sec-info compares the two models.

## Choosing the Margin Family {#sec-family}

```{r}
fam_pool <- fcmp$pooled |> filter(reference == "published", model != "margin_only")
fam_lab <- c(published = "Normal (published)", student_t = "Student-$t$", contaminated = "Contaminated normal")
fam_abl <- c(student_t = "Student-t margin", contaminated = "Contaminated-normal margin")
```

The family $\mathcal{D}$ of @eq-lik was chosen on out-of-sample predictions: in a backtest of model variants on a fixed set of snapshots during development, the normal beat the Student-$t$ on mean absolute error and log loss, and the contaminated normal tied it on log loss without improving the spreads and fitted more slowly. @tbl-family repeats the comparison with the evidence of this paper: the ablation backtest of @sec-ablation on every snapshot of `r sl(min(abl_seasons))` to `r sl(max(abl_seasons))`, and PSIS-LOO at each complete season's final posterior under the published priors, pooled over seasons (the sum of the per-season differences, with the root sum of squared standard errors).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-family
#| tbl-cap: "Margin families. Backtest: difference from the normal in mean absolute error (points) and log loss on the same games, with standard errors clustered by snapshot (positive is worse). LOO: pooled difference in $\\widehat{\\mathrm{elpd}}$ from the normal over complete seasons (positive is better), and the seasons in which it is positive. Tied: seasons whose observed share of games tied after regulation lies outside the 90\\% predictive interval."
tied <- fam_ppc |> filter(statistic == "Share tied after regulation") |>
  group_by(model) |> summarise(out = sum(observed > rep_hi | observed < rep_lo), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
tibble(model = names(fam_lab)) |>
  left_join(fam_pool |> select(model, diff, se, seasons, seasons_better), by = "model") |>
  left_join(tied, by = "model") |>
  mutate(dm = map_chr(model, \(m) if (m == "published") "--" else { x <- abl_d(fam_abl[[m]], "err_abs"); sprintf("%+.3f (%.3f)", x$diff, x$se) }),
         dl = map_chr(model, \(m) if (m == "published") "--" else { x <- abl_d(fam_abl[[m]], "logloss"); sprintf("%+.4f (%.4f)", x$diff, x$se) })) |>
  transmute(Family = fam_lab[model], `$\\Delta$ MAE` = dm, `$\\Delta$ log loss` = dl,
            `$\\Delta\\widehat{\\mathrm{elpd}}$` = ifelse(is.na(diff), "--", sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt(diff, 0), fmt(se, 0))),
            `Seasons better` = ifelse(is.na(diff), "--", paste0(seasons_better, "/", seasons)),
            Tied = paste0(out, "/", n)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrr")
```

`r { lt <- fam_pool; best <- lt$model[which.max(lt$diff)]; if (max(lt$diff) > 2 * lt$se[which.max(lt$diff)]) paste0("By LOO the ", tolower(gsub("\\$", "", fam_lab[[best]])), " fits the final posterior better than the normal in ", lt$seasons_better[which.max(lt$diff)], " of ", lt$seasons[which.max(lt$diff)], " seasons, by ", fmt(lt$median_diff[which.max(lt$diff)], 0), " in a typical season (", fmt(max(lt$diff), 0), " pooled, standard error ", fmt(lt$se[which.max(lt$diff)], 0), "; ", { ps <- fcmp$per_season |> filter(model == best); top <- ps[which.max(ps$diff), ]; if (top$diff > 0.4 * sum(ps$diff)) paste0(fmt(top$diff, 0), " of it from ", sl(top$season), " alone, standard error ", fmt(top$se, 0)) else "spread over the seasons" }, "), while the backtest favours ", if (abl_d(fam_abl[[best]], "logloss")$diff > 0) "the normal" else "neither clearly", ". The two answer different questions: LOO scores the density of every observed margin given the season's other games, including the tails that a heavier-tailed law fits better, while the backtest scores the spread and the win probability of the next week's games, which depend on the location and the scale. The published ratings and the resume use the win probability, so the backtest decides.") else paste0("Neither alternative beats the normal by LOO by more than two standard errors, and the backtest favours the normal or ties it, so the simpler family is kept.") }` None of the families reproduces the share of games tied after regulation (@sec-ppc): the spike at zero is a property of how close games end, which a continuous location-scale law of any of these shapes does not reproduce (@sec-discussion).

# Out-of-sample Evaluation {#sec-backtest}

## Design {#sec-bt-design}

Every Division I game is predicted by the latest snapshot before it: the preseason snapshot predicts the first days of the season, each Monday's posterior the games of the following week, and so on. By construction (@sec-pipeline) a snapshot contains no information from its own date or later. This is a rolling-origin evaluation [@tashmanOutofsampleTestsForecasting2000] with one origin per week, covering every game of every complete season from `r sl(first_season)` to `r sl(last_full)`, the conference and national tournaments included. Predictions are scored by the absolute error of the spread, the continuous ranked probability score of the predictive distribution of the margin, and the Brier score [@brierVerificationForecastsExpressed1950] and log loss of the home win probability, all strictly proper except the absolute error [@gneitingStrictlyProperScoring2007]. Two references are scored on the same games. The closing betting line is the sharpest public forecast available, since it aggregates information --- injuries, rest, motivation --- that no ratings model sees [@levittWhyAreGambling2004]; beating it is not the aim, and coming close to it with public results alone is evidence that the ratings are sound. Torvik's ratings as they stood the day before each snapshot, from the site's archive, give a second reference built from the same kind of data: Torvik's adjusted offensive and defensive efficiencies and tempos turn into a spread by the usual multiplicative formula, with a home-court advantage and a margin scale estimated from earlier seasons only.

## Accuracy {#sec-bt-accuracy}

```{r}
open_d <- params |> filter(kind == "preseason") |> select(season, opening = snap_date)
btw <- btg |> left_join(open_d, by = "season") |>
  mutate(week = as.integer(floor(as.numeric(game_date - opening) / 7)) + 1L)
bt_period <- btg |> group_by(period) |> score_bt()
bt_pl <- lined |> group_by(period) |>
  summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(actual - pred_margin)), mae_line = mean(abs(actual - line)), .groups = "drop")
sci <- split(bts$score_ci, bts$score_ci$metric)
```

@tbl-backtest scores every predicted game of the complete seasons, overall and by part of the season, and @tbl-backtest-line compares the model with the closing line and with Torvik on the games that have both.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-backtest
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling out-of-sample accuracy, all predicted Division I games of the complete seasons. MAE and RMSE are errors of the predicted margin in points; CRPS scores the predictive distribution of the margin, in points; Brier score, log loss and accuracy score the home win probability."
bind_rows(bt_all |> mutate(scope = "All games"), bt_period |> mutate(scope = ifelse(period == "Nov-Dec", "November--December", "January--April"))) |>
  transmute(Games = scope, N = fmt(games), MAE = fmt(mae, 2), RMSE = fmt(rmse, 2), CRPS = fmt(crps, 2),
            Brier = fmt(brier, 4), `Log loss` = fmt(logloss, 4), Accuracy = pct(accuracy, 1)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-backtest-line
#| tbl-cap: "The model against the closing line and against Torvik's ratings at the same date, on the games with a line (and, for Torvik, with Torvik ratings for both teams). The line's win probability is normal around the line with the standard deviation of earlier seasons' line errors. ATS is the share of games in which the model's side of the line covered, pushes excluded; the break-even rate against a standard $-110$ price is 52.4\\%."
tibble(
  Comparison = c("Model vs. closing line", "Model vs. Torvik"),
  Games = c(fmt(bt_line$games), fmt(bt_tv$games)),
  `MAE, model` = c(fmt(bt_line$mae, 2), fmt(bt_tv$mae, 2)),
  `MAE, other` = c(fmt(bt_line$mae_line, 2), fmt(bt_tv$mae_tv, 2)),
  `Log loss, model` = c(fmt(bt_line$logloss, 4), fmt(bt_tv$logloss, 4)),
  `Log loss, other` = c(fmt(bt_line$logloss_line, 4), fmt(bt_tv$logloss_tv, 4)),
  ATS = c(pct(bts$ats[["rate"]], 1), "--")
) |> ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Over all `r fmt(bt_all$games)` predicted games the mean absolute error is `r fmt(bt_all$mae, 2)` points (95\% interval `r fmt(sci$mae$lo, 2)`--`r fmt(sci$mae$hi, 2)`), the Brier score `r fmt(bt_all$brier, 4)` (`r fmt(sci$brier$lo, 4)`--`r fmt(sci$brier$hi, 4)`) and the log loss `r fmt(bt_all$logloss, 4)` (`r fmt(sci$logloss$lo, 4)`--`r fmt(sci$logloss$hi, 4)`), and the favourite wins `r pct(bt_all$accuracy, 1)` of the time. Games predicted by the same posterior share its errors, so these intervals come from a bootstrap that resamples whole snapshots, and the comparisons below use standard errors clustered the same way. On the `r fmt(bt_line$games)` games with a closing line the model's error is `r fmt(bt_line$mae, 2)` points against the line's `r fmt(bt_line$mae_line, 2)`. The difference, `r fmt(bts$dm_mae_line[["mean"]], 3)` points per game with standard error `r fmt(bts$dm_mae_line[["se"]], 3)` ($z = `r fmt(bts$dm_mae_line[["z"]], 1)`$ in a Diebold--Mariano comparison of absolute errors [@dieboldComparingPredictiveAccuracy1995]), is `r if (abs(bts$dm_mae_line[["z"]]) > 2) "distinguishable from zero: the market is better, though by little" else "not distinguishable from zero"`. Its win probabilities are `r if (bts$dm_brier_line[["mean"]] > 0) "worse" else "better"` than the line's (Brier difference `r fmt(bts$dm_brier_line[["mean"]], 4)`, $z = `r fmt(bts$dm_brier_line[["z"]], 1)`$). Against the line the model picks the covering side in `r pct(bts$ats[["rate"]], 1)` of `r fmt(bts$ats[["n"]])` games (95\% interval `r pct(bts$ats[["lo"]], 1)`--`r pct(bts$ats[["hi"]], 1)`), `r if (bts$ats[["lo"]] > 0.5) "above the 50\\% of a forecast with no edge on the market, but" else "consistent with the 50\\% of a forecast with no edge on the market and"` short of the 52.4\% needed to profit at standard prices. Against Torvik's ratings at the same dates the model's absolute error is `r fmt(abs(bts$dm_mae_torvik[["mean"]]), 3)` points `r if (bts$dm_mae_torvik[["mean"]] < 0) "smaller" else "larger"` ($z = `r fmt(bts$dm_mae_torvik[["z"]], 1)`$) and its log loss `r fmt(1000 * abs(bts$dm_logloss_torvik[["mean"]]), 1)` $\times 10^{-3}$ `r if (bts$dm_logloss_torvik[["mean"]] < 0) "smaller" else "larger"` ($z = `r fmt(bts$dm_logloss_torvik[["z"]], 1)`$), on the same `r fmt(bt_tv$games)` games.

@fig-bt-week shows how accuracy evolves through the season. The error is largest in the first week, predicted from the preseason information alone, and falls through November and December as the games accumulate. The gap to the line is `r { g1 <- bt_pl$mae[bt_pl$period == "Nov-Dec"] - bt_pl$mae_line[bt_pl$period == "Nov-Dec"]; g2 <- bt_pl$mae[bt_pl$period == "Jan-Apr"] - bt_pl$mae_line[bt_pl$period == "Jan-Apr"]; if (g1 > g2 + 0.01) "largest early" else if (g2 > g1 + 0.01) "smaller early than late" else "about the same early and late" }` (`r fmt(bt_pl$mae[bt_pl$period == "Nov-Dec"] - bt_pl$mae_line[bt_pl$period == "Nov-Dec"], 2)` points in November and December, `r fmt(bt_pl$mae[bt_pl$period == "Jan-Apr"] - bt_pl$mae_line[bt_pl$period == "Jan-Apr"], 2)` from January)`r { g1 <- bt_pl$mae[bt_pl$period == "Nov-Dec"] - bt_pl$mae_line[bt_pl$period == "Nov-Dec"]; g2 <- bt_pl$mae[bt_pl$period == "Jan-Apr"] - bt_pl$mae_line[bt_pl$period == "Jan-Apr"]; if (g1 > g2 + 0.01) ", when the market knows more about rosters than a regression on last season's numbers can." else ": the preseason regression keeps up with the market's knowledge of rosters, and the market's edge lies in what it learns during the season and the ratings do not see." }` The log loss *rises* from January, and the right panel shows why: conference play pairs more evenly matched teams, so the predicted probabilities move towards one half and every forecast, the line's included, is less certain.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bt-week
#| fig-cap: "Rolling out-of-sample accuracy by week of the season (week 1 is the first seven days, predicted from the preseason). Left: mean absolute error of the model's spread, of the closing line and of Torvik's ratings, on the games with all three. Centre: log loss of the model's and the line's win probabilities. Right: sharpness, the mean of $|p - 1/2|$ over the model's predicted probabilities. Weeks with fewer than 200 games are omitted."
#| fig-scap: "Out-of-sample accuracy by week"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.38
wk <- btw |> filter(!is.na(line), !is.na(pred_torvik)) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(n = n(), Model = mean(abs(actual - pred_margin)), `Closing line` = mean(abs(actual - line)),
            Torvik = mean(abs(actual - pred_torvik)), ll_m = mean(ll(p_home, home_win)), ll_l = mean(ll(p_line, home_win)),
            sharp = mean(abs(p_home - 0.5)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 200)
bind_rows(
  wk |> select(week, Model, `Closing line`, Torvik) |> pivot_longer(-week) |> mutate(panel = "MAE (points)"),
  wk |> transmute(week, Model = ll_m, `Closing line` = ll_l) |> pivot_longer(-week) |> mutate(panel = "Log loss"),
  wk |> transmute(week, Model = sharp) |> pivot_longer(-week) |> mutate(panel = "Sharpness")
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("MAE (points)", "Log loss", "Sharpness")),
         name = factor(name, levels = c("Model", "Closing line", "Torvik"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, value, colour = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model = col_power, `Closing line` = col_ref, Torvik = col_ink)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Model = "solid", `Closing line` = "solid", Torvik = "dashed")) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Week of the season", y = NULL)
```

**The predictive distribution of the margin.** A spread is a point forecast; the model also implies a predictive distribution of the margin, normal with the standard deviation implied by its win probability, which combines the uncertainty in the ratings at the snapshot with the game noise. Its central 50\%, 80\% and 95\% intervals contain `r knitr::combine_words(pct(bts$coverage$cover, 1))` of observed margins, and its continuous ranked probability score is `r fmt(bt_all$crps, 2)` points. The slope of the observed margin on the predicted one is `r fmt(bts$slope, 3)` (the line's: `r fmt(bts$slope_line, 3)`), so the spreads are neither too bold nor too timid.

**Totals.** The tempo model of @sec-tempo predicts the final combined score, overtime included, as the over/under is settled. On the `r fmt(bt_tot$games)` games with an over/under its mean absolute error is `r fmt(bt_tot$mae, 2)` points against the over/under's `r fmt(bt_tot$mae_line, 2)`. The gap, `r fmt(bt_tot$mae - bt_tot$mae_line, 2)` points, is `r if (bt_tot$mae - bt_tot$mae_line > bt_line$mae - bt_line$mae_line) "larger" else "smaller"` than the gap on the spread: pace and shooting depend on who plays, and the market knows the injury report.

## Calibration {#sec-calibration}

A win probability is useful to the resume only if it is calibrated, because $\WAB$ subtracts $\pi_g$ from an observed result. @fig-calibration groups all predicted games into ten fixed-width bins of their win probability and compares the mean prediction in each bin with the observed frequency, overall and by part of the season.

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of out-of-sample home win probabilities. Games are grouped into fixed-width bins of predicted probability; each point is a bin's mean prediction and observed home win rate, with a 95\\% binomial interval. The diagonal is perfect calibration. Left: all games. Right: November--December and January--April."
#| fig-scap: "Calibration of out-of-sample win probabilities"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.5
calib <- function(d) d |> mutate(bin = cut(p_home, seq(0, 1, 0.1), include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(bin, .add = TRUE) |> summarise(pred = mean(p_home), obs = mean(home_win), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(obs * (1 - obs) / n), lo = pmax(obs - 1.96 * se, 0), hi = pmin(obs + 1.96 * se, 1))
cal <- calib(btg)
cal_all <- bind_rows(cal |> mutate(split = "All games", panel = "All games"),
                     calib(group_by(btg, split = ifelse(period == "Nov-Dec", "November-December", "January-April"))) |>
                       mutate(panel = "By part of season"))
cal_all |>
  ggplot(aes(pred, obs, colour = split)) +
  geom_abline(colour = col_faint, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.4, position = position_dodge(width = 0.03)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.03)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`All games` = col_power, `November-December` = col_ref, `January-April` = col_power)) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted home win probability", y = "Observed home win rate")
cal_off <- cal |> mutate(z = (obs - pred) / se) |> filter(abs(z) > 2)
ct <- bts$calibration_tests
```

Every bin lies within `r fmt(100 * max(abs(cal$obs - cal$pred)), 1)` percentage points of the diagonal, but with `r fmt(bt_all$games)` games a gap of a point can be real. `r if (nrow(cal_off)) paste0(nrow(cal_off), " of the ", nrow(cal), " bins are more than two standard errors from it: ", paste0(as.character(cal_off$bin), ", predicted ", fmt(cal_off$pred, 3), " against observed ", fmt(cal_off$obs, 3), " ($z = ", fmt(cal_off$z, 1), "$)", collapse = "; "), ".") else "No bin is more than two standard errors from it."` The expected calibration error, the game-weighted mean gap between prediction and outcome within bins, is `r fmt(ct$ece, 3)`, and Spiegelhalter's test [@spiegelhalterProbabilisticPredictionPatient1986] gives $z = `r fmt(ct$spiegelhalter_z, 1)`$`r if (ct$spiegelhalter_z < -2) ": the predictions are slightly too cautious, the observed outcomes a little further from one half than predicted" else if (ct$spiegelhalter_z > 2) ": the predictions are slightly too confident, the observed outcomes a little closer to one half than predicted" else ""`. The caution is the posterior's: averaging the win probability over the uncertainty in the ratings pulls it towards one half, and early in the season, when that uncertainty is largest, the spreads are slightly over-shrunk as well (the slope of the margin on the spread is above one in November and December). A recalibration of the log-odds fitted on earlier seasons only, which sharpens them by about five percent, improved the log loss by less than $10^{-3}$ in development, too little to be worth the extra step, and is not applied.

The calibration of predicted games bears on the resume only indirectly. The bubble probabilities $\pi_g$ of @eq-wab use the same predictive law, but they describe a hypothetical fixture --- the bubble team against the opponent --- and are computed in sample, from the posterior that includes the game itself; no outcome can check them directly. That the model's out-of-sample probabilities for real fixtures are close to calibrated, in conference play especially, is supporting evidence that the scale of $\pi_g$ is right, not proof.

@fig-bt-season repeats the comparison with the line and with Torvik season by season. The gaps are stable, which suggests they reflect information the market has and the model does not rather than a drifting model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bt-season
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample mean absolute error by season on the games with a closing line and Torvik's ratings: the model, the closing line and Torvik on the same games."
#| fig-scap: "Out-of-sample error by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.36
btg |> filter(!is.na(line), !is.na(pred_torvik)) |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(Model = mean(abs(actual - pred_margin)), `Closing line` = mean(abs(actual - line)),
            Torvik = mean(abs(actual - pred_torvik)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-season) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("Model", "Closing line", "Torvik"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(season, value, colour = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model = col_power, `Closing line` = col_ref, Torvik = col_ink)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Model = "solid", `Closing line` = "solid", Torvik = "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = complete, labels = \(x) substr(sl(x), 6, 7)) +
  labs(x = "Season (tournament year)", y = "MAE (points)")
```

## Ablations and Baselines {#sec-ablation}

Each component of the model is tested by removing it and repeating the rolling backtest on the same games. Refitting every snapshot of every season for each variant is expensive, so the ablations cover the `r length(abl_seasons)` most recent complete seasons, `r sl(min(abl_seasons))` to `r sl(max(abl_seasons))` (`r fmt(abl_sum$games[abl_sum$variant == "Published model"])` games), with shorter chains than the published fits (two chains of 400 draws; the predictions are posterior means, for which that is ample). The published configuration is refitted the same way, so every row of @tbl-ablation is comparable.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ablation
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Rolling out-of-sample accuracy of model variants, every Division I game of ", sl(min(abl_seasons)), " to ", sl(max(abl_seasons)), ", each predicted by the snapshot before it. Each variant changes one thing. $\\\\Delta$ columns: difference from the published model on the same games, with a standard error clustered by snapshot; positive is worse.")'
abl_sum |>
  left_join(abl_diff |> filter(metric == "err_abs") |> select(variant, d_mae = diff, se_mae = se), by = "variant") |>
  left_join(abl_diff |> filter(metric == "brier") |> select(variant, d_b = diff, se_b = se), by = "variant") |>
  left_join(abl_diff |> filter(metric == "logloss") |> select(variant, d_l = diff, se_l = se), by = "variant") |>
  mutate(variant = factor(variant, levels = union(ablation_order, variant))) |>
  arrange(variant) |>
  transmute(Variant = as.character(variant), MAE = fmt(mae, 3), `Log loss` = fmt(logloss, 4),
            `$\\Delta$ MAE` = ifelse(is.na(d_mae), "", sprintf("%+.3f (%.3f)", d_mae, se_mae)),
            `$\\Delta$ Brier $\\times 10^3$` = ifelse(is.na(d_b), "", sprintf("%+.2f (%.2f)", 1000 * d_b, 1000 * se_b)),
            `$\\Delta$ log loss $\\times 10^3$` = ifelse(is.na(d_l), "", sprintf("%+.2f (%.2f)", 1000 * d_l, 1000 * se_l))) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrr")
sig_worse <- abl_diff |> filter(metric == "err_abs", diff > 2 * se) |> pull(variant)
sig_better <- abl_diff |> filter(metric == "err_abs", diff < -2 * se) |> pull(variant)
```

`r if (length(sig_worse)) paste0("Removing a component makes the spreads measurably worse (by more than two standard errors) for: ", knitr::combine_words(tolower(sig_worse)), ".") else "No variant is worse than the published model by more than two standard errors in mean absolute error."` `r if (length(sig_better)) paste0("The published model is beaten by more than two standard errors by: ", knitr::combine_words(tolower(sig_better)), ".") else "No variant beats it by more than two standard errors."` The preseason information matters most, as expected in a season whose first month is played between teams that have barely played anyone: without it, `r fmt(abl_d("No preseason information", "err_abs")$diff, 2)` points of absolute error per game over the whole season. The margin-only model settles the question of @sec-info empirically: the efficiency likelihood changes the mean absolute error by `r sprintf("%+.3f", -abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$diff)` points and the log loss by `r sprintf("%+.2f", -1000 * abl_d("Margin only", "logloss")$diff)` $\times 10^{-3}$ (published minus margin-only). `r { a <- abl_d("Shot-quality efficiency", "err_abs"); l <- abl_d("Shot-quality efficiency", "logloss"); paste0("Against the pure shot-quality margin the luck-adjusted one is ", if (a$diff > 2 * a$se) "better on the spread" else "indistinguishable on the spread", " (", sprintf("%+.3f", a$diff), " points, se ", fmt(a$se, 3), ") and ", if (l$diff > 2 * l$se) "better" else if (l$diff < -2 * l$se) "worse" else "indistinguishable", " on the log loss (", sprintf("%+.2f", 1000 * l$diff), ", se ", fmt(1000 * l$se, 2), ", $\\times 10^{-3}$, shot-quality minus published)", if (l$diff > 2 * l$se || a$diff > 2 * a$se) ": actual two-point finishing carries information about strength that a shot model's average make rate for the same shot does not." else ".") }` Freezing ratings within the season (*static ratings*, $\phi = 0$) changes the mean absolute error by `r sprintf("%+.3f", abl_d("Static ratings", "err_abs")$diff)` points (se `r fmt(abl_d("Static ratings", "err_abs")$se, 3)`)`r { l <- abl_d("Static ratings", "logloss"); paste0(" and the log loss by ", sprintf("%+.2f", 1000 * l$diff), " $\\times 10^{-3}$ (se ", fmt(1000 * l$se, 2), ")") }``r { a <- abl_d("Static ratings", "err_abs"); l <- abl_d("Static ratings", "logloss"); if (a$diff > 2 * a$se || l$diff > 2 * l$se) ": the spreads barely change, but letting ratings drift measurably sharpens the win probabilities, which is what the resume uses" else ": with drift of the size estimated in @fig-tau the two are hard to tell apart, and the random walk is kept because it estimates how fast ratings should forget instead of fixing it at zero" }`.

The model can also be compared with a rating system built differently. Least-squares ratings on the margin per 100 possessions, refitted at every snapshot with a weak ridge penalty and a home-court term (the Massey method, unpooled and static) and turned into spreads with the same expected possessions, predict the same games from the first Monday on: mean absolute error `r fmt(mean(mass_cmp$err_abs_b), 2)` against the model's `r fmt(mean(mass_cmp$err_abs_m), 2)`, log loss `r fmt(mean(mass_cmp$logloss_b), 4)` against `r fmt(mean(mass_cmp$logloss_m), 4)`, on `r fmt(nrow(mass_cmp))` games (the least-squares win probabilities use a normal law with the error of earlier seasons, so the first season is not scored). Torvik's ratings, the stronger baseline, were compared above. At the end of each complete season the final power rating's rank correlation with Torvik's final ratings is `r fmt(min(ext_cor$rho), 3)`--`r fmt(max(ext_cor$rho), 3)`.

## Priors and Preseason Information Out of Sample {#sec-loso}

The leakage of pooling the priors over every season can be measured directly. The first snapshots of every complete season --- opening night and the first three Mondays --- refitted with priors pooled from the *other* seasons only predict the games until the next snapshot with a mean absolute error of `r fmt(mean(loso_cmp$e_l), 3)` points against `r fmt(mean(loso_cmp$e_m), 3)` for the published predictions of the same `r fmt(nrow(loso_cmp))` games, and a log loss of `r fmt(mean(loso_cmp$l_l), 4)` against `r fmt(mean(loso_cmp$l_m), 4)`: the leakage is `r if (abs(mean(loso_cmp$e_l) - mean(loso_cmp$e_m)) < 0.05) "negligible" else "measurable"` in the weeks where the priors matter most, and none at all later, when the data dominate them.

The preseason prediction $d_i$ is the largest single input of the first weeks (@tbl-ablation), and its sources can be compared without refitting. @tbl-preseason predicts every Division I game before each season's second Monday from the preseason information alone --- the difference of the two teams' preseason values plus the season's home-court advantage, in points with the game's possessions --- for each source, and correlates each with the final ratings.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-preseason
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Preseason sources, every Division I game before the second Monday of each season, predicted from the preseason value alone, and its correlation with the season''s final rating; ", sl(first_season + 1), " to ", sl(last_full), ". The published prior is the roster regression, fitted on earlier seasons only, where it has enough history, and the even blend before.")'
src_lab <- c(own = "Our final rating last season", torvik = "Torvik's preseason rating", blend = "Even blend of the two",
             published = "Published (roster regression)")
pre_src |> filter(season > first_season) |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(mae = weighted.mean(mae, games), cor = mean(cor_final), games = sum(games), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = names(src_lab))) |> arrange(source) |>
  transmute(Source = src_lab[as.character(source)], Games = fmt(games), MAE = fmt(mae, 2),
            `Correlation with final` = fmt(cor, 3)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrr")
pre_tab <- pre_src |> filter(season > first_season) |> group_by(source) |>
  summarise(mae = weighted.mean(mae, games), .groups = "drop") |> (\(d) setNames(d$mae, d$source))()
```

Our own final rating from last season is the weakest single source (`r fmt(pre_tab[["own"]], 2)` points), since college rosters turn over heavily from one year to the next; Torvik's preseason rating, which uses the incoming roster, is better (`r fmt(pre_tab[["torvik"]], 2)`), and the regression that combines both with the roster's turnover is `r if (pre_tab[["published"]] < min(pre_tab[c("own", "torvik", "blend")])) "the best" else "not the best"` (`r fmt(pre_tab[["published"]], 2)`). The transfer portal has made turnover larger and more uneven since `r sl(2021)`, which is what the roster terms --- the value of incoming transfers and of departing players --- are there to capture.

## Tuned Choices {#sec-tuned}

Every choice that was tuned or set from data is listed in @tbl-tuned, with the data it used. Several used the same seasons that the backtest reports, which makes the reported backtest slightly optimistic for those choices; @sec-loso bounds the effect for the pooled priors, and the preseason regression is fitted on earlier seasons only.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tuned
#| tbl-cap: "Every tuned or data-driven setting, how it was set, and whether the data overlap the reported backtest."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Setting, ~Value, ~`How set`, ~`Overlaps backtest`,
  "Pooled priors $\\omega, \\tau, \\phi, \\eta$", "Table~\\ref{tbl-priors}", "Random-effects pooling of vague-prior refits, all complete seasons (Equation~\\ref{eq-pool})", "Yes (Section~\\ref{sec-loso})",
  "Other structural priors", "Table~\\ref{tbl-priors}", "Weakly informative, on the scale of the sport", "No",
  "Margin family", "normal", "Development backtest of variants (Section~\\ref{sec-family})", "Yes",
  "Efficiency signal", "luck-adjusted", "Development backtest of variants", "Yes",
  "Preseason regression", "own, Torvik, roster", "Least squares on earlier seasons only", "No",
  "Two-season carry-over $\\beta_2$", "on", "Development backtest of variants", "Yes",
  "Garbage-time rule", "20 pts / 10 min, 15 / 5", "Judgement; tighter, looser and none within noise", "Yes",
  "Free-throw shrinkage", "40 attempts", "Judgement", "No",
  "Tempo model ratios, half-life", "Section~\\ref{sec-tempo}", "Weekly backtest of totals", "Yes",
  "Bubble", "last team in", "The committee's question (Section~\\ref{sec-bench})", "No",
  "Sampler and gates", paste0(cfg$chains, " chains, ", cfg$warmup, "/", cfg$sampling), "Conventional thresholds", "No"
) |>
  ktab(align = paste0(">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{", c("3.4cm", "3.2cm", "5.6cm", "2.2cm"), "}"))
```

# The `r sl(last_full)` Season {#sec-results}

This section uses the `r sl(last_full)` season to show what the two products look like and how they relate. Most of it uses Selection Monday, when the resume matters, and the final posterior, after the tournament.

```{r}
nc <- btg |> filter(season == last_full, tournament %in% "NCAA") |> slice_max(game_date, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
nc_snap <- board |> filter(season == last_full, snap_date == nc$snap_date)
nc_par <- params |> filter(season == last_full, snap_date == nc$snap_date)
r_h <- nc_snap$rating[nc_snap$team_id == nc$home_id]; r_a <- nc_snap$rating[nc_snap$team_id == nc$away_id]
nc_mu <- r_h - r_a + nc_par$hca * nc$site
nc_w <- nc$pred_poss / 70
nc_plug <- pnorm(nc_mu * sqrt(nc_w) / nc_par$sigma_game)
```

::: {.example}
The `r sl(last_full)` national championship game, `r esc(nc$home)` against `r esc(nc$away)` at a neutral site, was predicted by the posterior of `r format(nc$snap_date, "%B %e")`. There the posterior mean ratings were $`r fmt(r_h, 1)`$ and $`r fmt(r_a, 1)`$ points per 100 possessions, so the expected margin is `r fmt(nc_mu, 1)` per 100 for `r esc(nc$home)`; with `r fmt(nc$pred_poss, 1)` expected possessions from the tempo model, the predicted spread is `r fmt(nc$pred_margin, 1)` points. With $\bar\sigma = `r fmt(nc_par$sigma_game, 2)`$ at the posterior mean, the plug-in win probability is $\Phi(`r fmt(nc_mu, 2)` \times `r fmt(sqrt(nc_w), 3)` / `r fmt(nc_par$sigma_game, 2)`) = `r fmt(nc_plug, 3)`$. The published probability averages over the posterior draws instead, `r fmt(nc$p_home, 3)`, `r ifelse(abs(nc$p_home - 0.5) < abs(nc_plug - 0.5), "closer to one half", "further from one half")` because the uncertainty in the two ratings widens the predictive distribution. The predicted total was `r fmt(nc$pred_total, 1)``r if (!is.na(nc$total_line)) paste0(" against a closing over/under of ", fmt(nc$total_line, 1)) else ""`. The closing line had `r esc(nc$home)` `r if (is.na(nc$line)) "--- no line was recorded" else if (nc$line >= 0) paste("favoured by", fmt(nc$line, 1)) else paste("as a", fmt(-nc$line, 1), "point underdog")`, and the result was `r nc$home_score`--`r nc$away_score`.
:::

@tbl-top lists the top of the resume at Selection Monday.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-top
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("The ", sl(last_full), " resume at Selection Monday, top 25. $\\WAB$ with its 80\\% interval; the resume rank with its 80\\% rank interval; the power rating (per 100 possessions above an average Division I team) with its rank; quadrant-1 record; strength of record; and the NCAA tournament seed.")'
top <- sel_last |> arrange(resume_rank) |> slice_head(n = 25) |>
  left_join(sel_field |> filter(season == last_full) |> select(team_id, seed), by = "team_id")
top |>
  transmute(` ` = resume_rank, Team = esc(team), Record = paste0(wins, "--", losses),
            `$\\WAB$` = sprintf("%s \\,{\\scriptsize(%s, %s)}", fmt(wab, 2), fmt(wab_lo, 1), fmt(wab_hi, 1)),
            `Rank 80\\%` = paste0(round(wab_rank_lo), "--", round(wab_rank_hi)),
            Power = sprintf("%s (%d)", fmt(rating, 1), power_rank),
            `Q1` = paste0(q1_w, "--", q1_l), SOR = ifelse(sor < 0.001, "$<$0.001", formatC(sor, format = "g", digits = 2)),
            Seed = ifelse(is.na(seed), "--", seed)) |>
  ktab(align = "rllrrrrrr")
wid <- top |> slice_head(n = 16) |>
  summarise(res = median(wab_rank_hi - wab_rank_lo), pow = median(rank_hi - rank_lo))
```

The rank intervals are the point of reporting a posterior. @fig-intervals shows them for the top 25 in both products. Among the resume top 16 the median width of the 80\% rank interval is `r fmt(wid$res, 0)` places for the resume and `r fmt(wid$pow, 0)` for power. `r if (wid$res < wid$pow) "Resume ranks are the sharper, because once the results are fixed only the valuation of the opponents is uncertain, while power ranks describe strength itself." else "Resume ranks are not sharper than power ranks: the valuation of the opponents and the bubble is itself uncertain, and at the top of the order the resumes are close."`

```{r}
#| label: fig-intervals
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Posterior rank intervals at Selection Monday of ", sl(last_full), " for the top 25 of the resume. Points are the published ranks; bars the central 80\\% of the rank across posterior draws. Teams are ordered by resume rank.")'
#| fig-scap: "Posterior rank intervals, resume and power"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.75
top |>
  transmute(team = factor(team, levels = rev(team)),
            Resume_r = resume_rank, Resume_lo = wab_rank_lo, Resume_hi = wab_rank_hi,
            Power_r = power_rank, Power_lo = rank_lo, Power_hi = rank_hi) |>
  pivot_longer(-team, names_to = c("product", ".value"), names_sep = "_") |>
  mutate(product = factor(product, levels = c("Resume", "Power"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = team, colour = product)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.55, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = r), size = 1.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Resume = col_resume, Power = col_power)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50)) +
  labs(x = "Rank (1 = best)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
sc_df <- sel_last |> filter(!is.na(wab))
lo_fit <- loess(wab ~ rating, data = sc_df, span = 0.9)
sc_df <- sc_df |> mutate(resid = wab - predict(lo_fit, sc_df),
                         lab = ifelse(team_id %in% c(top$team_id[1:8], bubble$team_id, first_out$team_id), team, NA))
luck_cor <- cor(sc_df$resid, sc_df$luck)
```

@fig-scatter plots the two products against each other for every Division I team at Selection Monday. The relation is monotone but loose. The right panel shows what the scatter around the curve is: the vertical distance of each team from the curve against its *luck*, actual wins minus the wins its own rating would predict against its schedule (the sum of its win probabilities in each game under the posterior). The two are correlated at `r fmt(luck_cor, 2)`: teams above the curve have won more games than their strength predicts, usually close ones, and teams below it have lost them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Resume against power at Selection Monday of ", sl(last_full), ", all Division I teams. Left: the dashed line is zero Wins Above Bubble, teams above it did better than the bubble team would have with their schedule; the grey curve is a LOESS fit; labelled, the resume top 8, the last team in and the first team out. Right: each team''s distance above or below that curve against its luck, actual minus expected wins.")'
#| fig-scap: "Resume against power"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.5
p_sc <- sc_df |>
  ggplot(aes(rating, wab)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_ref) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = col_faint, linewidth = 0.6, span = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = resume_rank <= field_size_now), size = 0.9) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.2, colour = col_ink, na.rm = TRUE,
                           min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1, max.overlaps = 30) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = col_resume, `FALSE` = col_ref), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Power rating (per 100 possessions)", y = "Wins Above Bubble")
p_luck <- sc_df |>
  ggplot(aes(luck, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = col_faint) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = col_faint) +
  geom_point(colour = col_ref, size = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = col_ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Luck (wins minus expected wins)", y = "WAB above the curve")
p_sc + p_luck + plot_layout(widths = c(1.5, 1))
```

```{r}
six <- top$team[1:6]
traj <- board |> filter(season == last_full, team %in% six) |>
  mutate(team = factor(team, levels = six))
traj_w <- traj |> mutate(w80 = hi - lo) |> group_by(snap_date, kind) |> summarise(w80 = median(w80), .groups = "drop")
```

@fig-trajectory follows the power rating of the resume top six through the season. Preseason ratings come from the preseason prediction alone and are wide: the median 80\% interval is `r fmt(traj_w$w80[traj_w$kind == "preseason"], 1)` points per 100 on opening night, `r fmt(traj_w$w80[traj_w$kind == "selection"], 1)` at Selection Monday and `r fmt(traj_w$w80[traj_w$kind == "final"], 1)` after the tournament. With the random walk a rating can fall as well as rise late in the season, and the bands do not narrow to zero: the walk keeps adding uncertainty of $\phi$ per week while each game removes some.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Power rating through ", sl(last_full), " for the Selection Monday resume top six, with 80\\% posterior intervals; the first point is opening night and the last the final posterior after the tournament.")'
#| fig-scap: "Power rating trajectories"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.55
traj |>
  ggplot(aes(snap_date, rating)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = col_power, alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = col_power, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sel_date, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_faint) +
  facet_wrap(~team, nrow = 2) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Power rating (per 100)")
```

```{r}
od <- fin_last
best_off <- od |> slice_max(off, n = 1); best_def <- od |> slice_min(def, n = 1)
od_cor <- cor(od$off, -od$def)
```

@fig-offdef splits the final `r sl(last_full)` power ratings into offence and defence (@sec-tempo). The best offence by this measure is `r esc(best_off$team)`'s, `r fmt(best_off$off, 1)` points per 100 possessions against an average defence, and the best defence `r esc(best_def$team)`'s, `r fmt(best_def$def, 1)` allowed. Across Division I good offences and good defences `r if (od_cor > 0.2) "tend to go together" else if (od_cor < -0.2) "tend to exclude each other" else "are nearly unrelated"` (correlation of Off with $-$Def $`r fmt(od_cor, 2)`$), and teams with the same power rating can get there in very different ways: every point on one diagonal of the figure has the same Off $-$ Def.

```{r}
#| label: fig-offdef
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Offence and defence at the end of ", sl(last_full), ", all Division I teams: points scored and allowed per 100 possessions against an average team on a neutral floor. The defence axis is reversed, so better teams are up and to the right; dashed diagonals are lines of equal power rating, 10 points apart. Labelled, the final resume top 12.")'
#| fig-scap: "Offence and defence"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.7
od |>
  mutate(lab = ifelse(resume_rank <= 12, team, NA)) |>
  ggplot(aes(off, def)) +
  # On the reversed y scale the line Def = Off - p is -Def = -Off + p (abline works in scale space)
  geom_abline(intercept = seq(-40, 40, 10), slope = -1, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_faint, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = resume_rank <= 12), size = 0.9) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.2, colour = col_ink, na.rm = TRUE,
                           min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1, max.overlaps = 30) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = col_power, `FALSE` = col_ref), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Offence: points scored per 100", y = "Defence: points allowed per 100")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-agreement
#| fig-cap: "Spearman rank correlation between rankings of Division I teams, by week of the season, averaged over complete seasons. Correlations with the AP poll use the teams it ranks."
#| fig-scap: "Agreement between rankings"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.45
cr <- function(a, b) { ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b); if (sum(ok) < 5) NA_real_ else suppressWarnings(cor(a[ok], b[ok], method = "spearman")) }
agree <- board |>
  filter(season %in% complete, kind %in% c("weekly", "selection")) |>
  left_join(open_d, by = "season") |>
  mutate(week = as.integer(floor(as.numeric(snap_date - opening) / 7)) + 1L) |>
  group_by(season, week) |>
  summarise(`Resume vs. Colley` = cr(resume_rank, colley_rank), `Power vs. Colley` = cr(power_rank, colley_rank),
            `Resume vs. Power` = cr(resume_rank, power_rank), `Resume vs. AP` = cr(resume_rank, ap_rank),
            `Power vs. AP` = cr(power_rank, ap_rank), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-c(season, week)) |>
  group_by(week, name) |> summarise(rho = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(is.finite(rho), n >= 6)
agree |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("Resume vs. Colley", "Resume vs. AP", "Resume vs. Power", "Power vs. Colley", "Power vs. AP"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, rho, colour = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Resume vs. Colley` = col_resume, `Resume vs. AP` = col_resume, `Resume vs. Power` = col_ink,
                                 `Power vs. Colley` = col_power, `Power vs. AP` = col_power)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`Resume vs. Colley` = "solid", `Resume vs. AP` = "dashed", `Resume vs. Power` = "dotted",
                                   `Power vs. Colley` = "solid", `Power vs. AP` = "dashed")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Week of the season", y = "Spearman correlation")
ag <- function(nm, wk) mean(agree$rho[agree$name == nm & agree$week %in% wk])
```

@fig-agreement measures agreement between the products and the references by Spearman rank correlation among Division I teams, week by week, averaged over the complete seasons. The resume tracks the record-only Colley ranking closely (mean correlation `r fmt(ag("Resume vs. Colley", 2:4), 2)` in weeks 2--4 and `r fmt(ag("Resume vs. Colley", 15:18), 2)` in weeks 15--18) --- both are functions of the record --- and differs from it in how opponents and sites are valued. The power rating is less correlated with Colley (`r fmt(ag("Power vs. Colley", 2:4), 2)` early, `r fmt(ag("Power vs. Colley", 15:18), 2)` late), as it should be, because it uses margin and efficiency. Agreement with the AP poll, which ranks only 25 teams, is computed on those 25.

```{r}
dis <- sel_last |> filter(resume_rank > field_size_now) |> arrange(power_rank) |> slice(1)
dis_games <- sl_last$games |> filter(team_id == dis$team_id) |> arrange(game_date) |>
  mutate(opp = team_name(opp_id))
dis_losses <- dis_games |> filter(win == 0)
```

::: {.example}
The products disagree most for teams that are strong but lost games. At Selection Monday of `r sl(last_full)`, `r esc(dis$team)` had power rank `r dis$power_rank` (`r fmt(dis$rating, 1)` per 100) but resume rank `r dis$resume_rank`, at `r dis$wins`--`r dis$losses`. Its own posterior gave it `r fmt(sum(dis_games$p_win), 1)` expected wins against this schedule, so its luck was `r fmt(sum(dis_games$win) - sum(dis_games$p_win), 1)`; `r nrow(dis_losses)` losses, `r sum(abs(dis_losses$pts_for - dis_losses$pts_against) <= 5)` of them by five points or fewer, cost it `r fmt(sum(dis_losses$p_bench), 2)` wins of $\WAB$, while its `r sum(dis_games$win)` wins earned `r fmt(sum(1 - dis_games$p_bench[dis_games$win == 1]), 2)`. The power rating reads those losses as close games that a strong team loses sometimes; the resume counts them as losses.
:::

## The `r sl(last_full)` Field {#sec-field}

```{r}
fl <- sel_field |> filter(season == last_full)
fl_tab <- sel_last |>
  left_join(fl |> select(team_id, seed, auto), by = "team_id") |>
  left_join(b0_last |> select(team_id, picked), by = "team_id") |>
  mutate(in_field = !is.na(seed), picked = coalesce(picked, FALSE)) |>
  filter((in_field & !auto) | picked) |>
  arrange(resume_rank)
in_not_model <- fl_tab |> filter(in_field, !picked)
out_model <- fl_tab |> filter(!in_field, picked)
```

The first question a reader will ask of a resume is whether it picks the teams the committee picked. Given the actual automatic bids, the `r n_al_last` at-large places of `r sl(last_full)` filled by $\WAB$ at Selection Monday would have taken `r sum(fl_tab$in_field & fl_tab$picked)` of the committee's `r sum(fl_tab$in_field)` at-large teams. `r if (nrow(in_not_model)) paste0("Chosen by the committee but not by $\\WAB$: ", paste0(esc(in_not_model$team), " (resume ", in_not_model$resume_rank, ", seed ", in_not_model$seed, ")", collapse = "; "), ". ") else ""``r if (nrow(out_model)) paste0("Chosen by $\\WAB$ but not by the committee: ", paste0(esc(out_model$team), " (resume ", out_model$resume_rank, ", power ", out_model$power_rank, ")", collapse = "; "), ".") else ""` @fig-pfield shows how early the season simulation knew: the probability of a place in the field that each snapshot gave every team, against whether the team was selected.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pfield
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of the season simulation's probability of a place in the NCAA tournament field, every team at every snapshot of the complete seasons with a tournament, by month of the snapshot; the last panel is Selection Monday, when only the at-large choices remain uncertain. Points are bins of predicted probability with a 95\\% binomial interval; the label gives the Brier score."
#| fig-scap: "Calibration of the probability of making the field"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.36
pf <- board |>
  filter(season %in% unique(sel_field$season), kind %in% c("weekly", "selection"), !is.na(p_field)) |>
  left_join(sel_field |> transmute(season, team_id, made = 1), by = c("season", "team_id")) |>
  mutate(made = coalesce(made, 0),
         when = ifelse(kind == "selection", "Selection Monday", format(snap_date, "%B"))) |>
  filter(when %in% c("December", "January", "February", "Selection Monday")) |>
  mutate(when = factor(when, levels = c("December", "January", "February", "Selection Monday")))
pf_bins <- pf |> mutate(bin = cut(p_field, c(-0.001, 0.02, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.98, 1))) |>
  group_by(when, bin) |> summarise(pred = mean(p_field), obs = mean(made), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(obs * (1 - obs) / n), lo = pmax(obs - 1.96 * se, 0), hi = pmin(obs + 1.96 * se, 1))
pf_brier <- pf |> group_by(when) |> summarise(b = mean((p_field - made)^2), .groups = "drop")
pf_bins |>
  ggplot(aes(pred, obs)) +
  geom_abline(colour = col_faint) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = col_resume, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(colour = col_resume, size = 1.2) +
  geom_text(data = pf_brier, aes(x = 0.02, y = 0.97, label = paste0("Brier ", fmt(b, 3))), hjust = 0, size = 2.6, colour = col_ink) +
  facet_wrap(~when, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Predicted P(in the field)", y = "Selected")
```

## The Resume Against the Committee {#sec-validate-resume}

A retrodictive ranking has no future outcome to score it against, so the evidence for the resume has to be external. @tbl-committee compares the rankings with the committee's choices in every complete season with a tournament: the number of the committee's at-large teams that each ranking's top at-large candidates include (given the actual automatic bids), the rank correlation with the seed lines over the field, and the correlation of our $\WAB$ with Torvik's on Selection Monday. It also reports retrodictive accuracy: the share of the season's decided Division I games whose winner the final ranking places higher.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-committee
#| tbl-cap: "The resume against the committee, by season, at Selection Monday: at-large teams the committee chose that each ranking's top at-large candidates include, out of the number of at-large places; Spearman correlation of $\\WAB$ and of the power rating with the seed (sign reversed); and Spearman correlation of our $\\WAB$ with Torvik's, all teams."
rv$committee |>
  transmute(Season = sl(season), `At large` = at_large, `By $\\WAB$` = overlap_wab, `By SOR` = overlap_sor,
            `By power` = overlap_power, `Seed $\\rho$, $\\WAB$` = fmt(seed_cor_wab, 2), `Seed $\\rho$, power` = fmt(seed_cor_power, 2),
            `$\\rho$ with Torvik's WAB` = fmt(torvik_wab_cor, 3)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrr")
cm <- rv$committee
rt_acc <- rv$retro |> group_by(system) |> summarise(a = weighted.mean(retro_acc, games), .groups = "drop")
ra <- setNames(rt_acc$a, rt_acc$system)
```

Over `r nrow(cm)` tournaments, $\WAB$'s at-large candidates include `r fmt(sum(cm$overlap_wab))` of the committee's `r fmt(sum(cm$at_large))` at-large teams (`r pct(sum(cm$overlap_wab) / sum(cm$at_large))`), strength of record's `r fmt(sum(cm$overlap_sor))` and the power rating's `r fmt(sum(cm$overlap_power))`. The disagreements are a handful of teams each year, at the edge of the field, where the committee weighs things a resume measure does not --- quadrant records, road records, the eye test, injuries --- and where the posterior itself is uncertain: the last few teams in and the first few out have overlapping $\WAB$ intervals (@fig-intervals). `r if (sum(cm$overlap_wab) > sum(cm$overlap_power)) "The committee selects on results, as the resume does, more than on strength." else "The committee's choices are no closer to the resume than to the power rating."` The seeds, which rank the whole field, follow $\WAB$ (median rank correlation `r fmt(median(cm$seed_cor_wab), 2)`) `r if (median(cm$seed_cor_wab) > median(cm$seed_cor_power)) "more closely than" else "no more closely than"` the power rating (`r fmt(median(cm$seed_cor_power), 2)`). Our $\WAB$ and Torvik's, built with different ratings and a differently defined bubble, agree almost perfectly (median `r fmt(median(cm$torvik_wab_cor, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`). Retrodictive accuracy at the end of the season is `r pct(ra[["WAB"]], 1)` for the resume, `r pct(ra[["SOR"]], 1)` for SOR, `r pct(ra[["Colley"]], 1)` for Colley and `r pct(ra[["Power"]], 1)` for power`r if (ra[["Power"]] < min(ra[c("WAB", "SOR", "Colley")])) ": a ranking built from the record explains the record better than one built to predict" else ""`.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The design principle of this paper is that a ranking should say which question it answers, and that different questions can share a model without sharing a formula. The power rating and the resume come from one posterior and are never mixed: the resume borrows the model's estimate of how hard each game was, and nothing else. That separation has a cost --- two numbers where the public expects one --- but each number can then be checked against something observable: the power rating against future games (@sec-backtest), and the resume, less directly, against the committee's selections and the season's own results (@sec-validate-resume). Basketball is kinder to the power model than football: thirty games a season, seventy possessions a game, and a play-by-play rich enough to separate what a team controls from how its shots happened to fall. The model comes within `r fmt(bt_line$mae - bt_line$mae_line, 2)` points of the closing line on average, `r if (bts$dm_mae_torvik[["mean"]] < 0) "ahead of" else "behind"` a widely used public rating built from the same games.

**Limitations.** Several choices deserve more work.

1. *The end of close games.* The model underpredicts the share of games tied after regulation (@sec-ppc), and no location-scale family removes the misfit (@sec-family). The end of a close game is played to the score: fouling, three-point attempts to tie, holding for the last shot. A likelihood for the regulation margin that respects the integer score and puts mass at zero --- a rounded or interval-censored version of the present one, or a model for the two scores themselves [@karlisAnalysisSportsData2003; @baioBayesianHierarchicalModel2010] --- would fit the centre of the distribution, at the price of a likelihood that is no longer conjugate to the efficiency margin's. It would matter for the spread more than for the win probability.
2. *One step size for every team and week.* The random walk of @eq-walk moves every team by Gaussian steps of the same size, so a team that loses its best player in February is pulled down only gradually, and a slow decline and a sudden one look alike. Heavier-tailed steps, or steps informed by the injury report and by minutes lost, would let a rating jump; one season identifies even one step size only weakly (@sec-hierarchy), so such extensions need informative structure rather than more parameters alone.
3. *Asymmetric garbage time.* The efficiency margin excludes garbage time, but the scoreboard margin cannot: a team that leads by 25 and rests its starters concedes late points that enter $y_g$ but not $e_g$. The model can absorb that only in $\lambda$ and $\kappa$, which are therefore averages over close and lopsided games.
4. *Priors from the whole history.* The pooled priors use every complete season (@sec-priors), and the leave-one-season-out comparisons of @sec-loso bound what that borrows. The non-pooled priors are weakly informative and set by judgement, and the game-level ones are irrelevant; the preseason loadings $\beta$ and $\beta_2$ are not, and could be pooled like the hierarchy's scales.
5. *A separate tempo model.* Possessions and totals come from a ridge regression outside the Bayesian fit (@sec-tempo), so their uncertainty is not propagated into the spreads and the offence--defence split, and the margin and the total are not modelled jointly. Folding tempo into the posterior would make the spread's uncertainty complete.
6. *Games are exchangeable.* Rest, travel, injuries, altitude and the size of the crowd are all absent, and home court is one number per season for every arena (@fig-tau); the gap to the closing line, which persists through the season (@sec-bt-accuracy), is a measure of how much these and roster knowledge matter.
7. *The committee is not modelled.* The season simulation's at-large selection is by projected $\WAB$, a stand-in for a committee that reads team sheets, not a model of it. Its probabilities of a place in the field are well calibrated (@fig-pfield) because the committee's choices and the resume largely agree, and they will be wrong in the same places where the two disagree.

-->

```{r, supp-setup}
fit_short <- c(first = "First Monday", final = "Final")   # in figures (the pdf device has no en dash)
```

# Appendix: Supplementary Posterior Checks {#sec-supp .appendix}

The snapshots of @sec-computation are checked by gates and summaries only, because keeping every draw of `r fmt(n_snap)` fits is not needed for publication. This appendix examines two posteriors in full, following the checklist of @kahleOverviewBayesianComputation2022 and @miyakawaPracticalComparisonBayesian2025 for applied Bayesian computation --- sampler behaviour; convergence; posterior geometry; the justification of informative priors and the priors they induce on derived quantities; sensitivity of the posterior to changes in the prior; predictive adequacy; and influence --- together with the visual workflow of @gabryVisualizationBayesianWorkflow2019. The two posteriors bracket the range the pipeline fits:

- **`r fit_lab[["first"]]`**: `r fmt(sup$first$n_games)` Division I games, about `r fmt(2 * sup$first$n_games / sup$first$n_teams, 1)` per team. The data barely constrain a team's strength, the hierarchy and the preseason prediction do most of the work, and this is where the hierarchical geometry is hardest for the sampler.
- **`r fit_lab[["final"]]`**: all `r fmt(sup$final$n_games)` Division I games of the season, the tournaments included.

Both are refitted with the production settings of @sec-gates (`r n_chains` chains, `r fmt(S_draws / n_chains)` post-warm-up draws each, `r fmt(S_draws)` in all) by the `supplement` target.

## Sampler Behaviour Across All Snapshots {#sec-supp-all}

Before the two detailed fits, @fig-supp-gates shows the gate statistics of every snapshot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-supp-gates

Centre: the smallest bulk effective sample size, with the gate at 400. Right: wall-clock time of the fit, four chains in parallel. Filled points failed a gate."
#| fig-scap: "Gate statistics of every snapshot"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.36
fit_snaps |>
  left_join(open_d, by = "season") |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(snap_date - coalesce(opening, snap_date)) / 7) |>
  transmute(week, fail = !pass, `Max R-hat` = max_rhat, `Min ESS` = min_ess, Seconds = secs) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Max R-hat`, `Min ESS`, Seconds)) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("Max R-hat", "Min ESS", "Seconds"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, value)) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(name = factor(c("Max R-hat", "Min ESS"), levels = c("Max R-hat", "Min ESS", "Seconds")), g = c(1.01, 400)),
             aes(yintercept = g), linetype = "dashed", colour = col_power) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = fail), size = 1.1, colour = col_ink, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 19), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Weeks since opening night", y = NULL)
```
